bio.en: Caitlin Kalinowski is a sought-after builder who has worked with legendary makers like Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, and Sam Altman, and is focused on robotics, manufacturing, and physical-world AI.
bio.zh: Caitlin Kalinowski 是一位备受追捧的构建者，曾与 Steve Jobs、Mark Zuckerberg、Sam Altman 等传奇人物共事，目前专注于机器人、制造和物理世界的 AI。

summary.en: Caitlin argues that as what's possible behind a keyboard with AI saturates, the next frontier is the physical world—robotics, manufacturing, and reindustrialization. She shares what made Steve Jobs' bar for talent and excellence unwavering and how Sam Altman pushes people to think 100x bigger. The conversation covers why design for physical AI matters, the coming “meteor” of memory-price constraints, and national security implications of reindustrialization.
summary.zh: Caitlin 认为，当键盘后靠 AI 能做的事趋于饱和，下一个前沿是物理世界——机器人、制造和再工业化。她分享了 Steve Jobs 对人才与卓越毫不退让的标准，以及 Sam Altman 如何逼人把想法放大 100 倍。对话涵盖物理 AI 的设计为何重要、即将到来的“内存价格流星”约束，以及再工业化的国家安全含义。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: There's a dawning realization, especially in the lab, the acceleration is going so vertical that what you can do behind a keyboard with AI is going to saturate. When that happens, the next frontier is the physical world. Robotics, manufacturing, industrialization.
turns.zh: 有一种渐渐清晰的认知，尤其在实验室里——加速曲线太陡了，你在键盘后面用AI能做的事，终会饱和。到那时候，下一个前沿是物理世界。机器人、制造、工业化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Living in the future and designing it.
turns.zh: 活在未来，并设计它。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: There's probably more change in war than there is in consumer electronics in the next two years. We need to invest a lot more in drones than in aircraft carriers.
turns.zh: 未来两年，战争发生的变化可能比消费电子还多。我们得在无人机上投远比航母多得多的钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just imagine 100,000 drones coming out of China just at us.
turns.zh: 光想想十万个无人机从中国朝我们扑过来。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I do feel that we need to reindustrialize the country significantly to be safe in a military sense. I would really like to reteach ourselves how to make things at scale, how to be more independent, people that are your allies now may not be in the future.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，为了军事上的安全，我们必须大幅重新工业化这个国家。我很想重新教会自己怎么大规模制造东西、怎么更独立——现在的盟友，将来未必还是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You work with some of the most legendary successful builders, Steve Jobs, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman.
turns.zh: 你跟一些最传奇、最成功的建造者共事过：Steve Jobs、Mark Zuckerberg、Sam Altman。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Sam is really good at saying, "Why not more? Why not 100X or 10,000 X? You are thinking too small." For Steve, the bar he held for the company for technical talent and for excellence was not wavering.
turns.zh: Sam特别擅长说：'为什么不再多点？为什么不是100倍、10000倍？你想太小了。'对Steve来说，他为公司、为技术人才、为卓越设的那条线，从不摇摆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does it take to create a robot that feels human and connected?
turns.zh: 要造出一个让人觉得有人性、有连接感的机器人，需要什么？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: If you walk into a room and are robots just like, "..." It's creepy. You want these devices to be non-threatening, appear soft, reactive to you. Pixar, Disney are probably the world's best at doing this type of design work.
turns.zh: 如果你走进一个房间，机器人只是'……'，那很瘆人。你要这些设备不具威胁感、看起来柔软、对你有反应。皮克斯、迪士尼大概是做这种设计的世界最强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a meteor called memory prices that are coming for consumer hardware and robotics and physical AI.
turns.zh: 有一颗流星叫内存价格，正朝消费硬件、机器人、物理AI砸过来。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: We're in trouble as an industry.
turns.zh: 我们这个行业有麻烦了。

Every AI company and so many startups are launching building AI hardware products and Caitlin has been at the center of this emerging field for decades. This conversation goes in a lot of different directions, many that I did not expect, and I hope to do a lot more episodes on the hardware side of building over the next few months. Before we get into it, don't forget to check out lenny'sproductPass.com for an incredible set of deals available exclusively to Lenny's newsletter subscribers. With that, I bring you Caitlin Kalinowski. (00:02:35): Caitlin, thank you so much for being here. Welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天我的嘉宾是Caitlin Kalinowski。Caitlin是硅谷最受追捧、也最有成就的硬件负责人之一。她是初代Unibody MacBook Pro团队的一员，也是苹果MacBook Air和Mac Pro的技术负责人。她在Meta领导了AR眼镜硬件团队，包括最先进的AR产品Orion背后的团队。此前她执掌Meta的VR硬件团队，帮忙设计了Rift、Quest等一众神级VR设备。最近她在OpenAI，从零帮组建了机器人和硬件部门。机器人和硬件、物理AI现在火得不行，每家AI公司、无数创业公司都在发AI硬件产品，而Caitlin在这个新兴领域站了几十年的中心。这期走向很多我没想到方向，未来几个月我想多做几期硬件侧的。开始前，别忘了去lennysproductpass.com，那是专属Lenny newsletter订阅者的超值优惠合集。说完，请出Caitlin Kalinowski。（00:02:35）Caitlin，非常感谢你来，欢迎上播客。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Thank you so much for having me. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 太谢谢邀请我。很兴奋能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to go in a bunch of different directions. I'm going to bounce around. I want to talk about VR. So much money, so many resources, so many smart people have been working on VR for so long. Meta spent, I don't know, $10 billion. They renamed the company, Meta, to lean into VR as the future of this metaverse that we're going to be living through. Feels like a lot of people are leaning out now. It feels like Meta's stepping back. Apple's stepping back with the Vision Pro. In spite of the incredible hardware that everyone, that you built, that your team built, just ... I've got a couple of the devices, it's just like a magical experience that you've ... Unlike anything you've ever experienced. It still has not caught on. What happened? Is there still a future where VR catches on or is the future kind of AR and something else?
turns.zh: 我们要走很多不同方向。我会跳着聊。我想聊VR。这么多钱、这么多资源、这么多聪明人搞了这么久VR。Meta花了，我不知道，100亿美元。他们改名叫Meta，押注VR就是我们即将生活的元宇宙的未来。但感觉现在很多人都在退。Meta在退。苹果用Vision Pro也在退。尽管有那些神级硬件——你建的、你团队建的，我手里有几台，那体验像魔法，跟你经历过的任何东西都不一样。它还是没火起来。发生了什么？VR还有没有火的那天，还是未来属于AR和其他东西？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I don't think I would've guessed exactly what happened here, but the way I look at it is VR helped us understand how to orient things in space relative to a simulated world and the real world and connect those two. We figured out SLAM, which was how to do positioning in space using cameras. We figured out a lot of depth applications of depth sensors. We figured out how humans perceive visual data in space and all of that actually while it's great for VR and I think VR gaming is really interesting, it is kind of a niche, but I think it's an interesting niche. What I see now is in robotics, all of these technologies are being used because you need to understand how the robot is moving through space. You need to understand how far it is from everything. You need to understand if you're wearing a VR headset and driving the robot, it's the same real technology. (00:04:16): And so for me, I view it as a step in a long technological arc. And to be honest, as someone who's not using VR a lot right now, I'm really glad that we did it, but I don't think it ... I expected it to be big, obviously, or wouldn't have been working at Oculus. And I think maybe the social aspect of having something in front of your face is part of why it didn't take off. And I think that we learned of course with Google Glass how important that is as well. And so when we tried to make it social, it's hard to make it social when you have your face covered.
turns.zh: 我当初没料到会这样，但我的看法是：VR帮我们理解了怎么把东西在'模拟世界'和'真实世界'之间做空间定位、并连起来。我们搞出了SLAM——用摄像头做空间定位。我们搞出了深度传感器的很多应用。我们搞清了人类怎么在空间中感知视觉数据。这些对VR很好、VR游戏也很有意思，但它算个niche；不过我觉得是个有趣的niche。我现在看到的是：在机器人领域，所有这些技术都被用上了，因为你需要理解机器人怎么在空间中移动、离一切多远。你戴VR头显去遥控机器人，用的是同一套真实技术。（00:04:16）所以对我而言，它是一条长技术弧线上的一步。老实说，作为一个现在不怎么用VR的人，我很高兴我们做了，但我不觉得……我当初当然预期它会很大，不然也不会在Oculus干。我觉得脸上罩个东西让社交很难，也许是它没起飞的部分原因。Google Glass也让我们学到了这点有多重要。所以当我们想让它社交化时，脸被遮住就很难社交。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is interesting. So just like the investment and innovation that happened that went into VR has actually proven to be really useful. And so it feels like the companies that have put a lot of effort into that and money into that are ahead on the next step. So is that where you think things go? Where do you think things are going? Is it AR glasses? Is something else? What's the future of this?
turns.zh: 有意思。所以投进VR的那些投资和创想，其实被证明非常有用。于是那些在VR上砸了大钱大力的公司，在下一步领先了。所以这就是你觉得到哪去？你觉得往哪走？是AR眼镜吗？还是别的？这未来是啥？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I believe in AR glasses as part of the future because I do think looking down at your phone all the time is not great for us as social creatures. So if you can maintain social connections and get information, that's where I think we're headed. Orion, the AR glasses we worked on, I worked on most recently are a bit ahead of their time because they're using waveguides and MicroLED that are not quite ready for mass production. The yields just aren't there. The cost is still high. I think that's absolutely a path that AR glasses are likely to take. And as we figure out the input to those glasses, how do you communicate with them when you're on the move, when you're in public? How do you communicate quietly, silently with them? I think once we start to figure out some of those challenges that having a display that's mostly off that you can turn on when you want it to be on seems like part of the future. (00:06:10): So that's part of it. The other part is there's this lineage of technology going through VR and then AR and now in, I'm using the term robotics, physical AI, but you really have to step back and look at autonomous vehicles, drones, obviously robots, autonomy period, manufacturing. All of these technologies are going to need the same piece parts, the same pieces that we built in the AR/VR spectrum.
turns.zh: 我相信AR眼镜是未来的一部分，因为作为社会性生物，老低头看手机对我们不好。所以如果你能维持社交连接、又拿到信息，那才是方向。我们做的Orion AR眼镜，我最近参与的，有点超前，因为它用的波导和MicroLED还没到量产的时候。良率不够，成本还高。我觉得这绝对是AR眼镜可能走的一条路。等我们搞清这些眼镜的输入——移动时、在公共场合怎么跟它们沟通？怎么安静地、无声地跟它们沟通？我觉得一旦攻克其中一些挑战，一个大多时候关着、你想开才开的显示屏，像是未来的一部分。（00:06:10）这是一部分。另一部分是：一条从VR、到AR、到现在——我用'机器人'、'物理AI'这词，但你要退一步看自动驾驶、无人机、当然还有机器人、广义的自主、制造。所有这些技术需要的零件是同一套，就是我们在AR/VR谱系里建的那套。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting with VR. There's this idea with when you build product, there's always this question when something doesn't work. Is it just you executed it badly or the idea was just a bad idea and it's always hard to know. It feels like with the AR, it's just like so much effort was put into making it work just for a decade, many decades, and just has not worked. So it's nice that we know, okay, there's nothing we can really do right now to make this work. I completely agree with you. The issue is just like, "I don't want to sit on my couch disconnected from the world." And even if I could see people through it's just like, "Eh, I'm just going to ... I don't need this. It's not that big of a deal."
turns.zh: VR有意思的是：做产品时总有这问题——东西不行了，是你执行差，还是点子本身就是坏点子，永远难判断。感觉AR这边就是：为了做成，投入了十年、几十年那么大的努力，就是没成。所以好在你我知道'好吧，现在真没什么能立刻让它成的'。我完全同意你。问题就是'我不想瘫在沙发上跟世界断了联'。就算我能透过它看到人，也就'呃，我随便，我不需要这个，没那么大事'。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: In AR, you're going to just start getting more and more larger and larger displays. But the great thing about Orion is you've got a 70 degree field of view binocular. So with the prototype, you got to sense what this is really going to be like in the future. It's very hard to describe how it feels to use a pair of glasses like this, but when you do, you suddenly are like, "Oh, I feel immersed. The field of view is wide enough. I feel immersed." And it becomes pretty clear that I think this is part of where the future's headed.
turns.zh: 在AR里，你会开始有越来越大、越来越大的显示屏。但Orion牛的是它有70度视场的双目显示。所以原型机上，你能感受到未来真正会是什么样。很难描述用这种眼镜的感觉，但一旦用上，你会突然'哦，我沉浸了，视场够宽，我沉浸了'。这就相当清楚：我觉得这是未来方向的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's surprisingly hard about hardware? A lot of software companies, a lot of people are just like, "Okay, cool. We're going to build some hardware." That's the future, that's the moat now. And they get into it and they're like, "What the heck?" What are some things that maybe people don't think about when they think about, "Okay, we're going to build some hardware." What are some of the surprising challenges that come up?
turns.zh: 硬件难在哪，是反直觉的？很多软件公司、很多人说'好酷，我们要搞点硬件'，那是未来、那是护城河。然后进去'搞什么鬼？'当人们想'好，我们要搞点硬件'，有哪些他们没想到的、惊人的挑战？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I like to talk to computer science folks about it this way. So computer science folks, as you know, they write code and then they compile the code often and they run the code and debug it, but they can compile their code every day, every hour, whatever they need to do. In hardware, we only get to "compile our code" four or five times.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这么跟CS的人讲。CS的人，如你所知，写代码、经常编译、跑、debug，但他们想编译就编译，每天、每小时都行。在硬件，我们一辈子只能'编译代码'四五次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Four, five times a year or?
turns.zh: 一年四五次？还是？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Total.
turns.zh: 总共。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, ever.
turns.zh: 好，有生之年。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Right. So if you're building hardware, you redesign it in CAD for every major build and then you have to release it. And once it's released, you compile it the last time you release it for mass production. If it's a mass production device, that's it. You're done. You can't ship over their updates. (00:10:52): So we have a different approach. We have to have a different approach, which is more conservative. You have to do more of the reliability checks and tests in line with the program because once you compile that last time, you're done. You make all the parts, you put them together, they're out in the world. The only alternative is to ship something new to replace it a couple years later. And so we have to be more conservative and we have to take our time because if you think about it, a product that sells millions, if you have a graph of all the parts put together on any different part of the device, you have a curve, you're in the plus and minus three sigma or more. So meaning if you have two parts that go together, you're going to get the smallest version of this one and the largest version of this one and you're going to have to put those together across the board. (00:11:45): People don't think about this that much, but the part variance is pretty high. And so we've got to solve for that last half a percent in the process of building so that when we compile our last time, when we build our last time, it's done and we're going to have a high yield, we're going to be able to make them and make money on them effectively and we won't have very many returns. And so that's kind of the game that we're playing.
turns.zh: 对。所以做硬件，你在CAD里为每次大build重做设计，然后release它。一旦release，你为量产做的最后一次'编译'就定了。如果是量产设备，就完了。你不能发个更新覆盖。（00:10:52）所以我们有不同做法，必须更保守。你得在程序里做更多可靠性检查和测试，因为最后一次编译完就定了。你做出所有零件、装起来、出去了。唯一的替代是几年后发个新的替换。所以我们得更保守、更花时间，因为你想，一个卖几百万的产品，如果把所有零件的组合画成图，你会得到一条曲线，落在正负三西格玛甚至更多。意思是，两个零件要拼，你会拿到这个的最小版和那个的最大版，得全配上。（00:11:45）人不太想这个，但零件方差相当高。所以我们得在建造过程中把最后那半个百分点解决掉，这样最后一次编译、最后一次build时，就定了，良率高、能造、能有效赚钱、退货少。这就是我们玩的游戏。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds so hard and complicated. They're just like, "Software is so nice, you just write some code, ship it. It's great." Why do you think people are getting so into robots and hardware now? What's the driving trend?
turns.zh: 听起来好难好复杂。他们就是'软件真香，写点代码发了就完'。你觉得到底为什么大家现在这么迷机器人硬件？什么趋势在驱动？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. What I'm seeing in the AI world in San Francisco is there's a dawning realization, especially in the labs, I think that the acceleration is going so vertical that what you can do behind a keyboard with AI is going to saturate. And I don't know when it's going to saturate and nobody else knows either, but when that happens, the next frontier is the physical world. (00:12:45): And so what I see happening is the labs, big tech, startups are all realizing at the same time, "Okay, this is coming. We're going to have complex systems that can solve problems in the digital world very, very quickly. We already have them. They're going to get better and more comprehensive and more capable." If you think about that as a frontier, you could see the end of that tunnel. Now, I don't know when it's going to be again, but we can see that that's going to saturate at some point, or at least people think it will. And when that happens, the next frontier is hardware. The next frontier is robotics, manufacturing, industrialization, the sensing layer in the real world, the ability to move objects in the real world and eventually we hope space.
turns.zh: 对。我在旧金山AI圈看到的是：一种渐渐清晰的认知，尤其在实验室——加速太陡，键盘后用AI能做的事会饱和。我不知道什么时候饱和，别人也不知道，但到那时候，下一个前沿是物理世界。（00:12:45）所以我看到实验室、大厂、创业公司同时意识到'好，这要来了。我们会有复杂系统，能极快解决数字世界的问题。我们已经有了，它们会更好、更全面、更能干'。如果你把这当前沿，你能看到隧道尽头。现在我不知道又是什么时候，但能看到它终会饱和，或者至少人们这么认为。到那时候，下一个前沿是硬件。下一个前沿是机器人、制造、工业化、真实世界的感知层、在真实世界移动物体的能力，最终我们希望还有太空。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one of the most interesting lines of development is these humanoid robots, that's kind of like our meat brains are always more attracted to robots that look like us and act like us. There's a few companies very ahead. There's Optimus, Tesla, there's Figure, there's NEO, there's a few others. What's your sense on just the current state of these humanoids and kind of where ... I don't know, how close are we to humanoids being around us?
turns.zh: 所以最有趣的发展方向之一是这些人形机器人——我们的肉脑子总更被像我们、像我们动的机器人吸引。有几家很领先：Optimus、Tesla、Figure、NEO，还有几个。你对现在人形机器人的状态、我们离它们来到身边有多近，什么感觉？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: We might be close. I have, like many others, safety concerns about large, strong humanoids operating right next to people because we have to have enough data to show that that's safe. There are some designs and 1X NEO is a good example of this that have made significant safety considerations in their designs and pulled mass inwards essentially, which is a lot safer. Softer robots is safer.
turns.zh: 可能近了。我和很多人一样，对大而强的人形机器人紧贴人操作有安全顾虑，因为我们需要足够数据证明那安全。有些设计——1X的NEO是个好例子——在设计上做了重大安全考量，把质量往内收，这就安全得多。更软的机器人更安全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to clarify, you're saying they're lighter and so the impact of a robot hitting you is less.
turns.zh: 澄清一下，你是说它们更轻，所以撞到你的冲击更小。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. The part that might hit you, which in this case might be the arm, if it's lighter and softer ... There's two aspects, you have the arm moving through space and then you have the actuator that's rotating so you have to add up the energy essentially for both of those things. And so that's an impact thing that you have to worry about. Then you have to worry about the compliance of the arm. If it's just hard, then the impulse is high, but if it's soft and compressible, then the impulse is lower. And so you really have to be thinking about this when you have robots around people. (00:15:09): So in my world, in my worldview, the humanoid robots are still prototypes and they're advanced prototypes. What we need to do is show that this works at all, which is kind of where we're at right now. Once we have working prototypes, then usually, at least in my field, what you do is you continue to revise them to make them cheaper, easier to manufacture, higher yield and safer. And I think this is what's going to happen next. In my mind, they're not quite ready yet. Now you can get a Chinese robot that can do all kinds of things for you, but if you look at the booklet, it says, "Hey, no human can be within three feet of this robot." And you're not going to see very many robots that are strong enough to do meaningful work that don't have that warning right now.
turns.zh: 对。可能撞到你的部分，这case里可能是手臂，如果更轻更软……有两方面：手臂在空间移动，加上让手臂转的驱动器在转，所以你得把这两者的能量加起来。这是你要担心的冲击。然后你还要担心手臂的顺应性（compliance）。如果硬，冲量就高；如果软、可压缩，冲量就低。所以机器人旁边有人时，你真得想这个。（00:15:09）所以在我的世界观里，人形机器人还是原型，是先进原型。我们要先证明它能跑起来，这大概就是现在所处的阶段。一旦有了能用的原型，通常——至少我这领域——你会不断改它们，让它们更便宜、更易造、良率更高、更安全。我觉得接下来会发生这个。在我心里它们还没完全就绪。现在你能买到中国机器人做各种事，但你看说明书：'嘿，任何人类不得进入这机器人三英尺内。'你现在还看不到几个强到能做有意义工作、却又没这警告的机器人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. It's funny to hear that at the same time there's these nunchuck wielding robots in China doing dances with other folks. I've never thought about just that part of it, the impact they can have if they go awry. I want to come back to that, but just like timeline wise, what's your sense realistically when humanoid robots are walking around the streets in people's homes at scale?
turns.zh: 太有意思。好笑的是同时听到中国那些耍双节棍、跟人跳舞的机器人。我从没想过这一面——它们出岔子时的冲击。我想回到这点，但时间线上，你现实地觉得人形机器人什么时候会规模化走上街头、进人家家？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: At scale is the problem in my mind. At scale is a huge challenge. Now for me, my background at scale means millions usually, but let's even say hundreds of thousands. You've got to get a good design that's running. Then you've got to make it reliable enough that it can keep running day to day to day without a lot of human intervention or repair and that's its own problem. (00:16:47): But the first problem you have is supply chain and this is going to be something that I hope that we can talk about a little bit more, but every single part that goes into that robot's coming from somewhere and many of these parts may become more restricted or difficult to make and it may be harder to assemble the subassemblies and the meaningful parts of the robot here in this country. So there's a very complex supply chain dependency right now on robots like humanoids, but also other robots that we have to figure out. And a lot of people are trying to move production here to the United States, which is very challenging because we don't have great actuator companies here yet, for example.
turns.zh: 规模化是我心里的难题。规模化是巨大挑战。对我，规模化的背景通常意味着几百万，就算说几十万吧。你得有个跑得稳的设计，然后它得可靠到能日复一日跑、不需要很多人干预或维修，这本身是问题。（00:16:47）但你第一个问题是供应链——我希望能多聊点——那个机器人里的每个零件都来自某处，很多零件可能变得更受限、更难造，在这个国家把子组件和有意义的部件组装起来可能更难。所以现在对人形机器人、也对其他机器人，有套很复杂的供应链依赖要解开。很多人在试图把生产搬回美国，这极难，因为我们这还没有很好的驱动器公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the actuator is the little arm, I don't know ... How would you describe an actuator to a non-robotics person?
turns.zh: 驱动器就是小手臂，我不知道……对非机器人人士你怎么描述驱动器？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, the actuator is the motor. So you put power into it, electricity into it, and you get motion out of it.
turns.zh: 驱动器就是电机。你通电子进去，动子出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 酷。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: And most of these robots have a rotating rotor essentially that then has gearing on it that then powers the limb or powers the head or the fingers or whatever else. So they could be small, they could be large.
turns.zh: 大多机器人有个旋转的转子，上面有齿轮，驱动肢体、头、手指或别的。所以可大可小。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. I hear the word a lot and I'm like, " I don't know exactly what it means." So thank you for explaining it. I want to talk about the supply chain stuff more because I know you think a lot about this,- what's the state of the union on the supply chain for say robotics? What's going on? What are the pieces? What are the challenges?
turns.zh: 好，棒。我常听到这词，'我不太确定它啥意思'。谢谢解释。我想多聊供应链，因为我知道你很想这个——机器人供应链现状如何？在干嘛？有哪些环节？哪些挑战？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So the way to think about it is you can start with raw materials and magnets is a good place to start. So we need to be able to get the magnets, the raw magnets, for example. Then we need to be able to process them, then we need to be able to integrate them into actuators and build the actuators around them. Then we need to be able to integrate those actuators into subcomponents or robots themselves. And each layer of this chain has essentially been outsourced over the last 25 years to countries like China, like Japan, like Korea. (00:18:44): And full transparency, I've been part of that transfer of engineering knowledge to Asia. In Asia, the expertise has historically been scale and being able to build a lot of these parts at lower prices. We've had this kind of deal across these borders that this is how we're going to operate for the most part. Now, of course, there's things we make in this country still and of course there's design and AI that's made in Asia, but that's essentially where things have been for a long time. And in order to have a safe supply chain, we need to start to work on having some independence in these layers and these stacks.
turns.zh: 这么想：从原材料起，磁铁是个好起点。我们需要能拿到原料磁铁。然后要能加工它们，再整合进驱动器、围着它们建驱动器。然后把驱动器整合进子组件或机器人本身。这链条的每一层，过去25年基本都外包给了中国、日本、韩国这类国家。（00:18:44）坦白说，我也参与过把工程知识转到亚洲。在亚洲，专长历来是规模和低价造大量零件。我们这些边界间有种默契：大体上就这么运作。当然，这国家还造些东西，当然亚洲也有设计和AI，但那基本是长久以来的格局。要有安全的供应链，我们得开始在这些层和栈上有些独立性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's interesting that your focus is on these actuators. Is that the bottleneck, this very specific part of a robot?
turns.zh: 有趣的是你把焦点放驱动器上。那是瓶颈吗，机器人这非常具体的部件？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: It might be. So if we can't get the magnets, then we have to design new actuator types that maybe use different materials that may be larger that may not be as efficient in space. So that's important. And then the actuators themselves are important because if for some reason we can't buy them, then we don't get to make robots. So it's foundational. There are some foundational technologies like this all backed by material science, essentially breakthroughs. There's batteries of course. There's actuators. The raw parts, the die-cast parts, the machine parts are less critical. We think we can get those, but I think everyone, not just in this country, but around the world is starting to think about supply chain because you have these disruptions, whether it's COVID or war and you see how quickly things change.
turns.zh: 可能。如果我们拿不到磁铁，就得设计新型驱动器，可能用不同材料、可能更大、空间效率没那么高。所以重要。驱动器本身也重要，因为如果某种原因买不到，我们就造不了机器人。所以它基础。有些基础技术都靠材料科学，本质上的突破。当然还有电池。驱动器、原料、压铸件、机加工件没那么关键。我们认为能拿到，但我觉得不止这国家、全世界都在开始想供应链，因为有中断——无论COVID还是战争——你能看到变化多快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, stupid question. Why magnets? Why is that a part of the supply chain? Why do we need magnets?
turns.zh: 好，蠢问题。为什么磁铁？为什么它是供应链一环？为什么需要磁铁？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, so it's a great question. So you have a ring of magnets that are polar opposites and they go like this around the ring and then you have something in the center that rotates. And the way it rotates is you have alternating current essentially, and so the magnets make the rotor spin.
turns.zh: 好问题。你有一圈极性相反的磁铁，绕圈排，中间有个转的东西。它转的方式是你通交流电，于是磁铁让转子转。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. We need a YouTube lecture of here's how physics works. Okay, very cool. So when you talk about China, this is ... What I imagine, what I think about now is watching the war in Ukraine and Russia, just like drones, just like how crazy and different the world is now that you can build these little drones that go and blow people up. Robots are a part of that. It's just like such a existential threat to every country now. The ability to build these things at scale. What's your advice? What should we do? What should we change to thrive in this future and not be in trouble?
turns.zh: 哇。我们需要个YouTube物理课'这里是物理怎么运作的'。好，很酷。所以你聊中国——我想到的是看俄乌战争，就无人机，就现在世界多疯狂——你能造些小无人机去炸人。机器人是其中一部分。这对每个国家都是种生存威胁。大规模造这些的能力。你什么建议？我们该咋办、该改啥，才能在这个未来里活好、不栽？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Well, you mentioned drones. It's another good example. You need essentially the same technology to make the rotor spin on a drone as you do to make an arm move on a robot. It's essentially the same base technology and supply chain. So we need to, at least on the military side, have an independent supply chain as much as possible. I think that's important. I think every other country should do that as well, but I don't think that's specific to us. (00:21:46): I do feel that we need to reindustrialize the country significantly in order to be safe in a military sense. You really never know what's going to happen in the future and people that are your allies now may not be in the future. The allied West I think is going through a lot of geopolitical changes. There's a lot of shifting. And so I would really like to reteach ourselves how to make things at scale, how to make things at quantity, how to process raw materials, how to be more independent so that when COVID happens again or something else happens again, we're not in trouble and we're not unable to protect ourselves.
turns.zh: 你提到无人机。另一好例子。让无人机转子转的技术，本质上和让机器人手臂动的技术一样。同样的底层技术和供应链。所以至少在军事侧，我们要尽可能有独立供应链。我觉得重要。我觉得每个国家都该这么干，但不止是我们。（00:21:46）我确实觉得，为了军事安全，我们得大幅重新工业化这个国家。你永远不知道未来发生什么，现在的盟友将来未必是。西方盟友在经历很多地缘变化。所以在变。所以我很想重新教会自己怎么大规模制造、怎么定量制造、怎么加工原材料、怎么更独立，这样COVID再来或别的再来，我们不太栽、能保护自己。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I think about it also, is Marc Andreessen had this visual on some podcast of, just imagine 100,000 drums just coming out of China just at us, what do we do? We're not prepared for that. I don't want to spend all our time on this dark stuff, but it's this real thing.
turns.zh: 我也想，Marc Andreessen在某播客有个画面：就想象十万个鼓（drums，应为drones）从中国朝我们扑来，我们咋办？我们没准备好。不想在这黑暗话题上耗太久，但这是真事。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Well, and Palmer Luckey is a friend of mine and we don't agree on everything, but I do think that we agree on some important aspects of how we need to respond here. I think he's right to say that we need to invest a lot more in drones than in aircraft carriers. I think that is this old way of thinking, and these are important components of the military, but it's an old way of thinking of, "Hey, we have this and we have this and we have this and our planes come off here." It's like, no, AI is changing everything and military technology is changing incredibly fast. And the place to look at that is Ukraine where drones are being changed and updated every day rapidly with 3D printing. And this is, I think, the future of where war is headed, unfortunately. (00:23:34): And I view this as a very different era that we're entering into with very different ... This isn't new to anybody, but you're looking at what it costs for them to send out a missile and what it costs for us to stop it. And this is just you have to do the math every time. And right now we're losing on the math, which is fine for a certain amount of time, but the longer it goes, the less fine it is.
turns.zh: 对，Palmer Luckey是我朋友，我们不事事同意，但有些重要方面怎么回应，我觉得到一块了。我觉得他说得对：我们得在无人机上投远比航母多得多的钱。那是旧思维，这些虽是军事重要组件，但是旧的'我们有这个、有这个、飞机从这下来'的思维。不，AI在改变一切，军事技术变得极快。该看的地方是乌克兰，那里无人机每天用3D打印快速改、快速更。我觉得不幸这就是战争未来的走向。（00:23:34）我视这为非常不同的时代，非常不同……这对谁都不新，但你看着他们发一枚导弹的成本、我们拦它的成本。每次都得算账。现在账面上我们在输，一段时期还行，但越久越不行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you optimistic that we'll figure this out?
turns.zh: 你乐观我们会搞定吗？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, America is really good at figuring these things out. We have a pioneering kind of independent spirit and a great engineering culture, but we need to move.
turns.zh: 对。美国特擅长搞定这些事。我们有拓荒式的独立精神、极好的工程文化，但得动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that we started the conversation with VR. Palmer Luckey obviously famously started Oculus now. It's interesting how this is so connected. You think VR is this trivial thing that we're just playing games and such, but it's like the same person is now building Anduril, which is the leading, I don't know, war robot building hardware company.
turns.zh: 有趣的是我们开场聊VR。Palmer Luckey显然成名于Oculus现在。这连接好有趣。你觉得VR是玩游戏的琐碎东西，但同一个人现在在建Anduril——领先的，我不知道，军工机器人硬件公司。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. And I think we need a lot more of them. I've chosen not to work for companies that create lethal technology, but I think that it's good to have people who are willing to do that. And I think that it takes everyone to build the future that we want.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得我们需要更多这样的人。我选择不为造致命技术的公司工作，但我觉得有人愿意干是好的。我觉得建我们想要的未来需要所有人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to the AI safety piece, it's so interesting. I had a couple conversations like this on the podcast. We think about all this prompt injection and jailbreaking that happens with chatbots and none of people think about what if you propped inject a robot walking ...
turns.zh: 回到AI安全，太有趣。我在播客聊过几次这种。我们想 chatbots 的prompt injection、越狱，没人想如果给走路的机器人prompt inject会怎样……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like not enough people think about, what if you prompt inject a robot walking around and get them to punch someone? And we're so far from that feeling like we can actually stop that.
turns.zh: 就像不够多人想：如果给走路的机器人prompt inject，让它去揍人呢？而我们离能真正拦住这个还远得很。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. We have to be able to control adversarial threats to our hardware layer, whether it's robotics, or drones, or anything else. And that's going to be a huge part of the future of warfare.
turns.zh: 对。我们得能控制对我们硬件层——无论机器人、无人机还是别的——的对抗性威胁。那会是未来战争的大头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Just people talking about OpenClaw, and how much you ... Like you could just tell it, "Give me all your passwords," and it's done all these things to people's lives, and just like robots walking around, "Hey, okay, here's all this person's secrets."
turns.zh: 对。大家聊OpenClaw，你多……就像你跟它说'把你的密码都给我'，它就把人的生活的这些事全做了，就像机器人走来'嘿，好了，这人的所有秘密在这'。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: My OpenClaw story is I sandboxed it, so it's on its own computer, but I gave it three things. I gave it my real email address and my ... I don't know what it was. I gave it some information about one of my accounts or something like that. And I added it to the social media, I can't remember what it's called, the OpenClaw social-
turns.zh: 我的OpenClaw故事是：我把它沙箱化了，在它自己电脑上，但我给了它三样东西。我给了它我的真邮箱和我……不记得是啥。我给了它我某个账户的信息之类。我还加了它到社交媒体，不记得叫啥，OpenClaw的社交——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, Moltbook?
turns.zh: 哦，Moltbook？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. I added it to Moltbook and I was like, "Okay, whatever you do, don't share my private information, but go crazy." And five minutes later, all it had done is posted my personal email address. It was like the one thing it had.
turns.zh: 对。我加了它到Moltbook，说'好，随便你干，但别分享我的私人信息'。五分钟后，它干的唯一一件事就是把我私人邮箱发了出去。那正是它手里唯一的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nailed it.
turns.zh: 正中。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: And [inaudible 00:26:07] "Okay, you're shut down." It was so funny, no matter how careful you are with these things, you just can't really ... We're not at a place [inaudible 00:26:15]-
turns.zh: 然后（听不清00:26:07）'好了，你被关了'。太好笑，无论你多小心，就是没法……我们还不到那个程度（听不清00:26:15）——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which is exactly your point, that the robots can do a lot more damage. And they never thought about just the softness of their hand as a way to keep us safer.
turns.zh: 这正是你的点：机器人能造成大得多的破坏。而他们从没想过用'手的柔软'这种方式来保护我们更安全。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Nat Friedman just did this interesting talk at Stripe Sessions, and he's talking to his OpenClaw about drinking more water and sleeping better. And as he's driving in a self-driving car, it told him, "Okay, here, there's a place off the freeway that you should go to." And it changed the destination of his Tesla to take him there, because I imagine he connected it to their API at some point.
turns.zh: 哦天。Nat Friedman刚在Stripe Sessions做了个有趣talk，他跟他的OpenClaw聊多喝点水、睡好点。他开自动驾驶车时，它说'好了，高速外有个地方你应该去'，然后把它Tesla的目的地改了带他去那，因为我猜他某时把它连到了API。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: That's so funny. These are going to get weird fast, I think.
turns.zh: 太好笑。这些会很快变诡异，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So kind of on this thread of hardware emerging as a moat, as something people realize is a big part of the future to be competitive, AI labs, all these other companies, you've been at a company's ... You've been at Apple, which had a very great and long-lasting hardware program. Then you went to Meta where you helped build, basically bootstrap a hardware program from scratch. I feel like those lessons are very valuable to people trying to do that now. What was that experience like, helping Meta build a hardware program, and what are some lessons for people that are trying to do this at their company?
turns.zh: 好。顺着'硬件成为护城河、成为大家意识到是未来竞争力大头'这条线，AI实验室、所有那些公司，你在一些公司……你在苹果，有极好极长久的硬件项目。然后你去Meta，基本从零帮建了个硬件项目。我觉得那些教训对现在想干的人极有价值。帮Meta建硬件项目是什么体验，对想在公司干这事的人有什么教训？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So Apple has been best-in-class at this. There's a bunch of reasons. One, hardware is a first-tier citizen at Apple. There's a lot of companies where hardware isn't part of the core product development conversation as much, but that's an exception. Apple also taught me and a lot of other people actually, if you look at the era that I was there, I was very, very lucky, because if you look at the other folks who were there ... I was there between '07 and the end of 2012. If you look at the other people who were there working on these things, they actually have a lot of key positions now across the industry. (00:28:01): And I attribute that to how good Apple is at training people to think about complex interdependent decisions and risk. And I don't think I realized that they were doing that at the time, but if you look back, what you see is a real dedication to hardware excellence, the proper process to go through and do really good experiments in hardware, and figure out what the best outcome is. (00:28:32): But there's something underneath that, which is understanding the first principles of why are we building it this way, and what are the key outcomes we're looking for? And actually, John Ternus talked about this, I think, a few days ago, where he talked about the back of the cabinet. I don't know if you saw this video, but basically John said that he was impressed, that he learns from Steve Jobs that there's a cabinet maker who finished the back of the cabinet, and how important that was. (00:28:57): And that goes very, very deep at Apple, where every single design decision, even on the inside of the device, is considered. And this isn't just an aesthetic decision. What it does is actually force the engineering, industrial design operations community there to think about, "What are we really doing and what's the core of what's happening for this part, for this assembly, for this consumer product, and what really matters?" (00:29:24): And what happens is if you're that methodical, what really matters tends to rise out, and look very simple at the end. And so part of what you're seeing in many folks coming from that era is an understanding of how to do that, which in the very beginning of the Mac side, Macs didn't sell as many, and the quality wasn't quite as high, but by the end of that era, Macs were very popular and selling in much higher volumes. (00:29:55): And so I think that made a big difference. And I was only a small part of that. I was the thermal lead on the first MacBook Pro, and then over time worked to lead successive iterations of the MacBook Air, and the cylindrical Mac Pro. But I was lucky enough to work with these folks and learn from them, who'd been doing this for a really long time. (00:30:15): So you have to take those lessons, and then when you leave, try to distill them and explain them to a new community. Now, Oculus was actually a hacking hardware startup. Oculus started from folks who actually met on forums, you might know this, Lenny, who were hacking PlayStations or Super Nintendos into portable backpacks. (00:30:41): And so there was an ethos at the company that was actually quite good for the DNA of a hardware team. And then I was on the Meta side when we did the acquisition, and when we acquired them, they had that spirit of rapid iteration. They had made Crescent Bay before the acquisition, I think, but then to professionalize that, get the yields up, and get the volumes up was ... the cost down, was kind of the challenge we faced in the first Rift.
turns.zh: 苹果在这方面是顶级的。原因有几个。一，硬件在苹果是一等公民。很多公司硬件不是核心产品开发对话的一部分，但那是例外。苹果也教了我、教了很多人——看我在的那段：我是07到12年底在那。看当时在那搞这些事的其他人，他们现在行业里占了很多关键位。（00:28:01）我把它归因于苹果多会培训人去思考复杂的相互依赖决策和风险。我当时没意识到他们在做这个，但回头看，看到的是对硬件卓越的真 dedication、走正确流程做极好的硬件实验、搞清最佳结果是什么。（00:28:32）但底下还有东西：理解'我们为什么这么建'的第一性原理，以及我们要找的关键结果是什么？其实John Ternus几天前聊过这个，他讲柜子背面。你看过这视频吗？大体John说，他从Steve Jobs学到：有个 cabinet maker 把柜子背面也做完了，那有多重要。（00:28:57）这在苹果极深：每个设计决策，哪怕设备内部，都被考虑。这不只 aesthetic。它实际逼着那的工程师、工业设计、运营社区去想'我们到底在干啥、这零件、这组件、这消费产品核心是什么、什么真重要'。（00:29:24）如果你……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So on lesson I'm hearing here is being very detail-oriented. I don't know if that's the right word, just like, focus on every element of the end product. Because to your point, it's not just about that back of the cabinet, but I think about, it's like the brown M&M story, where like a band puts in the contract, you have to have brand M&Ms in the room, because that means they read it and it's not like the M&Ms matter, it's a test that they read the thing. And is that kind of the message there?
turns.zh: 我听到的教训是极度注重细节。不知道这词对不对，就是聚焦最终产品的每个元素。因为如你所说，不只是柜子背面，我想到棕色M&M故事——乐队在合同里写'房间里必须有品牌M&M'，因为那意味着他们读了合同，M&M不重要，是测试他们读没读。是那意思吗？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I think the message is understanding why you're doing what you're doing, and then every design decision supporting that goal. And that requires a lot of detail, and it requires a lot of persistence, and that requires a lot of consistency, but understanding why you're doing what you're doing and what the end goal is is, I think, the key, and letting that expand into not only the software and the UX, but also the hardware.
turns.zh: 我觉得信息是理解你为什么干这个，然后每个设计决策都支撑那目标。这需要很多细节、很多坚持、很多一致，但理解你为什么干、终点目标是啥，我觉得是关键，并让它扩展到不只软件UX，也到硬件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's an example of that, just to make it more concrete for us?
turns.zh: 举个具体点的例子？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: A great example is the Quest 2. So we reduced the Quest 2 price quite a lot, and what we had to do is understand, what are we trying to do? We're trying to democratize VR, we're trying to get VR to more people. And the only way we could do that is reduce the price. And so what it required is a redesign of the entire product, essentially, for cost, which then, I think, led to the highest-selling VR headset of all time. (00:32:37): And it's not easy, because you had to, in our case, remove cameras, remove components, change materials, change manufacturing processes. But when you have alignment that you want to get this to more people and the way to do that is to reduce the cost, then that kind of drives everything else. And it was still a very high-quality product with great, I think, low return rates, and it was a very strong product. Maybe even stronger than if we hadn't done that, funny enough, but it hit our price point.
turns.zh: 好例子是Quest 2。我们把Quest 2价格降了不少，要做的是理解'我们要干啥'——我们要让VR民主化、让更多人用上。唯一办法是降价。所以它要求 essentially 整个产品为成本重新设计，结果带来了史上销量最高的VR头显。（00:32:37）这不容易，因为我们得去掉摄像头、去零件、换材料、换制造工艺。但当你对齐'要让更多人用、办法是降成本'，那就驱动一切。它仍是极高质量产品，退货率很低，是强产品。可能比不降成本还强，好笑，但它命中了价格点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Coming back to just the question of, say a company's like, "Okay, we need to build some hardware. We're going to build our own glasses. We're going to build a little phone device and secretive thing," whatever OpenAI is up to. What other tips do you have? I know it's impossible to like, "Here's all you need to know," but just what else should people be thinking?
turns.zh: 好。回到那问题：比如公司说'好我们要搞硬件，我们要自己造眼镜、造个小手机设备和保密的东西'，无论OpenAI在搞啥。你还有啥tip？我知道不可能'这是你需要的全部'，但人们还该想什么？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Having your goals defined early and sticking to them is important. Hardware's not as adaptable to lots of changes throughout its development as anything digital. And so if you set out to say, "Okay, we want to make something that's $300," and then halfway through you say, "Oh, it actually has to be $150," you've almost burned a lot of that early time. (00:33:49): So you kind of need to have a sense of having pre-thought out what you want, and having those, I like to call them KPIs, but essentially goals written down, and try to change them as little as possible. So that is very tough. In fact, that may be the toughest thing. Because if you do that properly, and you have the right prioritization of those things, you know whether you can ship or not. You know whether you're done. (00:34:16): And in hardware, one of the challenges is, we talked about compiling four or five times. Every time you build and you iterate your design, that's another three months or four months or five months or whatever it might be. And so you're trying to time the feature set, with the quality, with the timing. (00:34:34): And in hardware, timing is important, because if you come out with your product a few weeks before your competitor, you might get all the PR, you might get all the interest. It's pretty brutal. And so each of those days that you ship before your competitor is worth a lot of money. It might be worth $10 million to you. I'm making this up. I don't know. So you have to balance that with how many times you iterate. And if you know what your goals are upfront and you hit them, then you know you can ship. And often engineers, and I'm guilty of this too, especially on the hardware side, never feel like they're done. (00:35:06): So this is a pretty nuanced thing. So that's one thing. The second thing is we tend to design the things that we know how to design first, and actually the right approach is to design the hardest parts first. One example will be, and there's no IP here, so I'm obviously not going to share any IP or anything internal, but at one point we had to route cables through a hinge in a device, in a laptop we were making. And because it wasn't clear that those cables would fit, that's where the architect started. And he looked at the diameter, and how to split the cables out, and made sure that they would fit before finalizing the hinge design. (00:35:45): A lot of people would start at the part they knew, like, "Oh, we're going to use this display, so I'm going to put this in CAD, and I'm going to do all this other stuff." But the architects who are the best actually look at where are the pinch points, where is this going to fail? And they start to do the detailed design there first. (00:35:58): And then a couple other points is, the part that your customer touches or interacts with the most needs way more iteration than everything else. So easy on a computer, you touch the trackpad the most, and then maybe the keyboard next. So those things have to be really good. They have to feel good, they have to respond properly, they have to be highly reliable, and then maybe the other pieces further out don't take quite as much iteration. So you have to boost your iteration on the things that people touch the most or interact with the most. So those are kind of some principles that I wrote about, but these are just things that you learn trying to build quickly. And the last piece that's really critical if you're making hardware for folks out there who are trying to make hardware is, you can't wait around, ever. (00:36:48): There's never enough time. So if you know that you need to do something, what I learned from folks like Shelly Goldberg at Apple now, who I think is a VP now, and Kate Bergeron when I was there at Apple is, you need to do it right now. Anything you know you need to do, you need to do right now, because in two days there's going to be a surprise coming around the corner that you need that time to fix. And so this sense of stacking the things that you know you need to do and just getting them out of the way, even if you technically have more time, is this kind of ruthless efficiency that I learned with them.
turns.zh: 早期定好目标并守住重要。硬件不如数字东西能在开发中随意改。所以如果你开头说'好，我们要做300美元的东西'，中途说'哦它其实得150美元'，你基本烧掉了早期很多时间。（00:33:49）所以你有点得预先想好你要啥，把那些——我喜欢叫KPI，但本质就是写下来的目标——尽量别改。这很难。其实那可能是最难的。因为如果你做对了，对这些事有正确优先级，你就知道能不能发、知不知道做完了。（00:34:16）硬件的挑战之一，我们聊过编译四五次。每次你build、迭代设计，又是三个月、四个月、五个月或更久。所以你在拿功能集、质量、时机做 timing。（00:34:34）硬件里时机重要，因为你比对手早几周出，可能拿到所有PR、所有关注。很残酷。你比对手早发的每一天都值很多钱。可能值1000万，我瞎编的。所以你得和迭代次数平衡。如果你 upfront 知道目标并命中，就知道能发。工程师——我也有罪——尤其硬件侧，从觉得'做完了'。（00:35:06）所以这是很微妙的事。这是一点。第二，我们倾向于先设计会设计的东西，而正确做法是先设计最难的部分。一例是，没有IP……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Let me just summarize your advice here. So one is be very clear on goals, I want to come back to this. Two is do the hardest part first, the riskiest piece, essentially, to physically build. Three is focus on the pieces that people will use most, say the trackpad, keyboard. I want to talk about that. And four is just like, do it now. Even if you think you have more time, you never know what's around the corner, and it's better-
turns.zh: 绝了。好，我把你建议总结下：一是目标极清晰，我想回头聊这个；二是先做最难、最有风险、物理上最难建的部分；三是聚焦人们用得最多的部件，比如触控板、键盘。我想聊这个。四是就现在做。哪怕你觉得还有时间，你永远不知道拐角有啥，最好——

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: You just don't. It's not even that you don't know what's around the corner. If you're working in hardware, you actually don't have more time.
turns.zh: 你就是不知道。不只是不知道拐角有啥。如果你干硬件，你其实没有更多时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. On the goals, what are kind of like buckets of goals? So cost is when you shared like, "We need this under $300." What are some other buckets of types of goals people should be thinking about?
turns.zh: 好。关于目标，有哪些目标类别？你说成本'我们要300美元以内'。还有啥类型的目标该想？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So in VR display resolution or arc minutes, like how many pixels per degree do you want is actually one of the key metrics. So you need to understand what your key metrics are. And why is that key? Well, that's your visual field. So you think about Retina displays on MacBooks. They figured out the KPI of what the human eye could see, probably overshot it a little bit, and built that. And then do you really need to keep as much engineering pressure up on the resolution of a display after that? Maybe not. (00:38:38): So VR's not there yet, not even close. Not in mass-produced VR, we don't have Retina displays yet. So that is one aspect of pushing that up is one example. I think on a computer, obviously you're talking about clock speed, you're talking about how many parallel processes you can run, you're talking about weight, you're talking about price, and you're talking about features. So when we did the MacBook Air, it became very clear, because we were machining it, that there are certain features, like ambient light sensor, that we just ... didn't make sense anymore. And so being willing to just jettison them for what we were going for, which was weight and size. So if you have those overarching goals, you can actually make decisions, engineering decisions pretty quickly. (00:39:24): And this is actually something that I think Elon, I've heard, does very well, is define the value of a gram of weight versus the cost, or he does, I've heard, engineering ratios, essentially and he's able to put numbers on what those ratios should be, which I think is really smart.
turns.zh: VR里，显示分辨率或角分（arc minutes），比如每度多少像素，其实是关键指标之一。所以你得懂你的关键指标。为什么关键？那是你的视场。想MacBook的视网膜屏，他们搞清了人眼能看到的KPI，可能略超，然后照那建。之后还要在分辨率上保持那么大工程压力吗？也许不。（00:38:38）VR还没到，差得远。量产VR里我们还没有视网膜屏。所以把这推上去是一例。电脑上，显然你说时钟速度、并行进程数、重量、价格、功能。所以我们做MacBook Air时，很清楚，因为我们是机加工的，有些功能比如环境光传感器，我们就是……没意义了。所以愿意为我们要的——重量和尺寸——把它们扔掉。所以如果你有那些总目标，你能很快做工程决策。（00:39:24）这其实是我觉得Elon据说很擅长的：定义一克重量对成本的价值，或他做工程比值，能给那些比值定数字，我觉得特聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So it's a very easy trade-off. "Okay, here's the formula telling us weight is less important in this case."
turns.zh: 有意思。所以是很容易的权衡。'好，这公式告诉我们这case重量没那么重要。'

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. And if you can do that, then the decisions fall out pretty easily.
turns.zh: 对。如果你能这样，决策就很好出了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of the Air and weight, I remember, I feel like there's a very classic moment in Steve Jobs lore where he comes out and has this manila envelope, and has the MacBook Air inside it, and then takes it out and everyone's like, "No way." Were you part of that? Was that something that people wanted to do from the beginning?
turns.zh: 说到Air和重量，我记得Steve Jobs传说里有个经典时刻：他拿个马尼拉信封出来，里面是MacBook Air，拿出来大家'不可能'。你参与了那个吗？那是大家从一开始就想要的吗？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I think, if my memory serves, the very, very, very first MacBook Air was a pretty low volume device that was machined, but kind of had more of a proof of what could be done. And that was the manila envelope one, I think, where the side door opened out to give you the port, and it had this shape underneath. (00:40:39): And then the next rev of that was the MacBook Air that we know, essentially which is wedge shaped, which is different. And so the wedge shape is the one that I worked on, and the one that went and hit more volume. But that manila envelope one was the one that proved you can CNC a computer. And so they each have really important roles in the roadmap.
turns.zh: 我记得，非常非常早的MacBook Air是低产量的机加工设备，更像证明能做到啥。那是马尼拉信封那个，我觉得，侧门打开给出端口，底下有那种形状。（00:40:39）下一版才是我们认识的、楔形（wedge）的MacBook Air，不一样。所以楔形是我做的、走量那个。但马尼拉信封那个证明了你能CNC一台电脑。所以它们在路线图里各有极重要的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to your point about focusing on things that people use the most, famously, Apple screwed up this keyboard. There was this butterfly keyboard situation for a long time. You're like, your eyes are closed [inaudible 00:41:16]. What happened? What happened, Caitlin?
turns.zh: 回到你'聚焦人们用得最多的东西'，著名的，苹果搞砸过这个键盘。有段时间蝴蝶键盘事件。你当时眼睛闭着（听不清00:41:16）。发生了啥？Caitlin，啥情况？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I didn't work directly on that keyboard, so I can't talk about what happened with it, but obviously this is something that you got to get right. And I will say, the modern MacBook keyboards are awesome and excellent, and I don't know what happened with that. I don't think those were devices I was working on at the time.
turns.zh: 我没直接做那个键盘，所以不能说它发生了啥，但这显然是你得搞对的事。我会说，现代MacBook键盘很棒很好，我不知道那发生了啥。我觉得那不是我当时在做的设备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nice. Safe. Marked safe. Along these lines, Apple's kind of famous for not listening to what people want. It's kind of like a classic thing with Steve Jobs. He's not walking around doing user focus groups, asking, doing user research, somehow continues to build incredibly popular products. What do you think they do right, or do they do a lot of user feedback sessions, things like that? How does it end up working out?
turns.zh: 漂亮。安全。标了安全。顺着，苹果出名的不听用户想要啥。Steve Jobs经典。他不到处做用户焦点小组、问用户研究，却 continues 建极受欢迎的产品。你觉得他们做对了啥，还是他们做很多用户反馈会之类？到底怎么成的？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I mean, I left over a decade ago, so I don't know what they're doing now in terms of user feedback. I think this one gets misinterpreted though, Lenny. I think that what is being said is if you want to build something new, customers don't know what they want, because they haven't seen it. (00:42:23): So a good example is the iPhone, which I didn't work on, but when you build a new iPhone with a touchscreen, you can't really go ask a hundred people what they want, because they're going to say a keyboard on their screen. And this is, I think, the ethos that you're getting at, which is, and this is true for anybody building a new product with a new feature. And I've tried to build, as much as I can, teams that work on products that have something new about them. (00:42:47): Either they're a new category, or there's a new manufacturing process, or something that hasn't been done before. And when you're thinking about this, you can't really use what you learned from the same field and the same product class. It just doesn't work, because you actually won't get the answer right. (00:43:05): And I think this is actually what Steve was talking about, which is, you can't get intuition if you're changing something fundamentally. Your customers won't know what they want because they haven't seen it. But if you show it to them, they will absolutely know that it's awesome and that is what they want. But if you get stuck in an iterative feedback cycle with your customers, it's very hard to go zero to one with something new. And so in my view, and I don't know for sure, I didn't talk to him about this, but that's my view of what that means.
turns.zh: 我十多年前就离开了，所以不知道他们现在用户反馈怎么做。但这点被误解了，Lenny。我觉得说的是：如果你想建新东西，客户不知道他们想要啥，因为他们没见过。（00:42:23）好例子是iPhone，我没做，但当你建带触屏的新iPhone，你不能真去问一百人想要啥，他们会说屏幕上也想要键盘。我觉得这就是你指的 ethos：对任何建带新功能新产品的人都成立。我尽量建有'新东西'的团队。（00:42:47）无论是新品类、新制造工艺、还是从前没做过的事。想这个时，你不能用同领域同产品类的老经验。就是不行，因为你答不对。（00:43:05）我觉得这正是Steve说的：在根本改变时你拿不到直觉。客户不知道想要啥因为他们没见过。但你给他们看，他们绝对知道'这太牛了、这就是我要的'。但如果你陷在和客户的迭代反馈循环里，很难从零到一去搞新东西。所以在我看来——我不确定——没跟他聊过这，但这是我的理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am so excited to tell you about this season's supporting sponsor, Vanta. Vanta helps over 15,000 companies like Cursor, Ramp, Duolingo, Snowflake, and Atlassian earn and prove trust with their customers. (00:43:52): Teams are building and shipping products faster than ever thanks to AI. But as a result, the amount of risk being introduced into your product and your business is higher than it's ever been. Every security leader that I talk to is feeling the increasing weight of protecting their organization, their business, and not to mention, their customer data. Because things are moving so fast, they are constantly reacting, having to guess at priorities, and having to make do with outdated solutions. (00:44:19): Vanta automates compliance and risk management, with over 35 security and privacy frameworks, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA. This helps companies get compliant, fast, and stay compliant. More than ever before, trust has the power to make or break your business. Learn more at vanta.com/lenny. And as a listener of this podcast, you get $1,000 off Vanta. That's vanta.com/lenny. (00:44:46): I'm going to go in a completely different direction. Coming back to components of hardware, I asked a bunch of people what to I talk to you about. One of the people is the founder of Matic, the CEO of Matic, Mehul Nariyawala. I've never said his last name out loud, so I hope I didn't butcher it. By the way, I love my Matic. I don't know if you have a Matic, but it's like-
turns.zh: 我超兴奋跟你讲本季支持赞助商Vanta。Vanta帮超过15000家公司——Cursor、Ramp、Duolingo、Snowflake、Atlassian——赢得并证明对客户信任。（00:43:52）团队借AI比以往更快建和发产品。但结果，引入产品的业务风险比以往都高。我聊的每个安全负责人都感到保护组织、业务、更别提客户数据的重量在加重。因为动太快，他们不停反应、得猜优先级、得凑合用过时方案。（00:44:19）Vanta自动化合规和风险管理，有超过35个安全和隐私框架，包括SOC 2、ISO 27001、HIPAA。帮公司快速合规、保持合规。比以往任何时候，信任都能决定你生意生死。去vanta.com/lenny了解。作为本播客听众，你省1000美元Vanta。就是vanta.com/lenny。（00:44:46）我要走个完全不同的方向。回到硬件组件，我问了一堆人该跟你聊啥。其中一个是Matic创始人、CEO Mehul Nariyawala。我从没大声念过他姓，希望没念残。顺便，我爱我的Matic。不知道你有没有Matic，但它就像——

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I have two, and I've purchased two more for friends.
turns.zh: 我有两台，还给朋友买了两台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, yeah. What an endorsement. Yeah. Basically, it's like this amazing robot vacuum that just works. So his question, so he wanted to ask you, and so he suggested to ask you this, is about memory prices. The way he described it is there's a meteor called memory prices that are coming for consumer hardware, and robotics, and physical AI. What's going on there?
turns.zh: 哦，绝了。什么级别的背书。对。基本就是个超好用的机器人吸尘器。所以他的、他建议问你的问题是内存价格。他描述是：有一颗流星叫内存价格，正朝消费硬件、机器人、物理AI砸来。那在搞啥？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, we are in trouble as an industry. And I'm not an expert on this, but I think that AI has to do with why. And I also think that the supply chain is constrained. I have been advising startups and companies to pre-buy memory, and to have enough memory in stock, if they can afford it, to ride out price spikes. (00:45:58): Like anything in this category, let's see, this happened in COVID too. So we had so many supply chain disruptions, and getting enough memory was one of the challenges. So we had to pre-buy as well. I won't say who, but the company I was working with had to pre-buy memory as well. And so this is part of what I wanted to talk to you about today, is these supply chain disruptions. And if a key component that goes into a lot of tech, like memory or silicon, is constrained, there's not much you can do. (00:46:32): You either pay, or you have already pre-bought enough that you can ride things out. And so those are the only real options. Obviously there's a risk to pre-buying, and the price might go down. And so the challenge is, I think, there's a latency with supply chain in something like memory, where it can't adapt fast enough, often, to demand, or there's a new category of product, or, in this case, maybe data centers, that are just eating up so much and are actually not as cost-sensitive as somebody in consumer electronics like Matic might be. And so they'll just pay for these higher costs. This is tricky and something we have to deal with all the time.
turns.zh: 对，我们这个行业有麻烦了。我不是这专家，但我觉得AI是原因之一。我也觉得供应链受限。我一直建议创业公司和公司预买内存、囤够内存（如果囤得起），扛过价格尖峰。（00:45:58）这类事，看，COVID时也这样。我们有那么多供应链中断，拿到够内存是挑战之一。所以我们也得预买。我不说谁，但我当时待的公司也得预买内存。所以我想今天跟你聊的就是这些供应链中断。如果进大量技术的关键组件，比如内存或硅，受限了，你没啥能做的。（00:46:32）你要么付钱，要么你已经预买够能扛过去。所以只有这两个真选项。当然预买有风险，价格可能降。挑战是，我觉得内存这类供应链有延迟，常常跟不上需求，或有新品类、或这case数据中心在吞掉大量、对成本没那么敏感（不像Matic这种消费电子），于是它们就付高价。这棘手，我们总得处理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much have prices gone up? How bad is this problem, and where do you think it'll go?
turns.zh: 涨了多少？这问题多糟，你觉得会去哪？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Actually, this is a great question, Lenny. I don't know what's going to happen. I think prices are going to double, probably. I don't know on what timeline. If I knew what timeline the prices were going to double on, I'd be trading, which I'm not very good at. I'd really be, I'd be doing a different job if I could predict these things, but certainly we're going to have a supply chain shock.
turns.zh: 好问题，Lenny。我不知道会发生啥。我觉得价格大概会翻倍。不知道时间表。如果我知道翻倍的时间表，我就在做交易了，我不擅长。我能预测这些就干别的了，但肯定会有供应链冲击。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's already gone up a lot. If you're saying it'll double, but it's already gone up. I don't know. I saw numbers like 6x and some like that.
turns.zh: 而且已经涨很多了。你说翻倍，但它已经涨了。我不知道。我看到过6倍这种数。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Oh, really? I didn't realize it was that bad.
turns.zh: 哦真的？我不知道那么糟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a number I saw, let's not quote that. And you're saying, yeah, from what I hear, it's AI-driven, just like you need ... And when you talk about memory, it's like DRAM and things. What is memory, when we talk about memory? What's going on there?
turns.zh: 那是我看到的数，别引用。你说，对，听说是AI驱动的，就像你需要……你聊内存，是DRAM这类。内存是啥，我们说内存时？那在搞啥？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Processing. So the way to think about it is processing memory. You think about memory on your hard drive or your solid state drive, where you're keeping files that you're not using, essentially, in many cases or that you're dealing with maybe documents or pictures that you have. Maybe that's in cold storage on a server, maybe that's using a hard drive somewhere. (00:48:18): This is usually things that you don't need really, really fast access on. But if you're running a program, some of that program is actually going to be run in RAM. And so there's different kinds, obviously, for servers. There's different kinds of server racks. Some server racks are actually focused on this type of memory, and some server racks are focused more on what we consider like a cold storage or a slower ... Now, this isn't my area of expertise, but certainly most of the products that I built, maybe all of them have had RAM, and we've had to figure out how to ... For me, mostly it's a packaging issue. Where do you put it? Does it need to be accessible? Which RAM do you pick? How fast does it need to be, and what is the cost? Is usually our trade-offs.
turns.zh: 处理。这么想：处理内存。你想硬盘或固态盘上的内存，你存不怎么用的文件，很多case或你处理的文档照片。可能在服务器冷存储，可能在某硬盘。（00:48:18）这些通常你不需要极快访问。但你跑程序时，部分程序其实在RAM里跑。所以有不同类型，服务器显然有不同类型机架。有些机架专注这类内存，有些专注我们说的冷存储或更慢的……这不是我专长，但我建的产品大多、可能全有RAM，我们得搞清怎么……对我大多是个封装问题。放手？要可访问吗？选哪种RAM？要多快，成本多少？通常是我们的权衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what is the bottleneck with more RAM? Is it just the companies that make memory are just not able to produce at this rate, because there's so much demand?
turns.zh: 更多RAM的瓶颈是啥？就是造内存的公司跟不上这速率，因为需求太大？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: That's right. That's exactly what's happened.
turns.zh: 对。正是发生了啥。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is a really good specific example of just how hard it is to build hardware. All it takes is one piece to be not available, and your whole thing's screwed.
turns.zh: 所以这是个好具体例子，说明造硬件多难。只要一个零件不到位，整个就完蛋。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, you can't build anything if you have one component missing.
turns.zh: 对，少一个组件你啥都造不了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's say Matic is an example. How many components are there that they all have to assemble and not have one not available?
turns.zh: 比如Matic是个例子。有多少个组件都得装齐、不能少一个？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I'm doing the math in my head. They probably have between 50 and 150 parts. It's possible that they have more. I haven't seen their CAD, so I don't know what it's like inside their device, but they do have a lot of things going on. They have the wheels of the device that are obviously moving around. Then they have a vacuum, but they also have a mop, and obviously they have a vacuum bag. They have the reservoir that-
turns.zh: 我心里在算。它们大概50到150个零件。可能更多。我没看过他们CAD，不知道设备内部，但它们事挺多。有显然在动的轮子。有吸尘，还有拖布，显然有集尘袋。有装液体的水箱——

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: They have a vacuum bag. They have the reservoir that the liquid has to go in for the mop. They have a system which I think is SLAM-based, which can see your room and make a map of it and identify which surface is which, and that, I believe, stays on the device, so it doesn't go up to the cloud, which is also what we did in VR as well, which I think is a good privacy practice. And then, they, of course, have wireless modules that connect up so you can communicate with your device. They're going to have a SoC silicon, they're going to have RAM, they're going to have PCBs. If you take everything off of those things like all the little caps off the PCBs and everything, then you're in the thousands of parts easily. So it depends on how you count, but this is not a simple device.
turns.zh: 有集尘袋。有拖布要用的液体水箱。有个系统，我认为是SLAM-based，能看房间、建地图、识别哪面是啥，而且我相信它留在设备上不上云，这也是我们在VR做的，我觉得是好隐私实践。然后当然有无线模块连设备。有SoC硅、有RAM、有PCB。把那些小电容全从PCB摘下，轻松上千零件。所以看你怎么数，但这不是简单设备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And all it takes is one piece to not be available.
turns.zh: 只要一个零件不到位。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. So imagine you're a vendor that sells you a component that's a die-cast component, goes out of business. You can get another die-cast component in three months maybe and at quantity in five months or something like that at high quantity. This is recoverable. If your silicon goes out, if you can't buy your silicon, you can't buy your chip. Now, you have to redesign your board, and you have to find something else that might work. This is a catastrophic redesign. If you can't get the RAM you wanted and the form factory you wanted, this is what I call a... Essentially, it's a catastrophic redesign. You now have to redesign the entire guts of your product and then secure supply chain for these new things, build it again on the production line, test it again, do all the reliability testing. It is non-trivial, and so this is why we care. (00:51:41): So there's a hierarchy of components. Often in consumer electronics, we start with silicon and the display, which are the longest lead time things usually in my world. In robots, actuators are pretty tricky to get, even just for prototyping. Sometimes it takes a month or two to buy an actuator.
turns.zh: 对。想象你是卖压铸组件的供应商，倒闭了。你可能三个月拿到另一个压铸件，量产可能五个月。这能恢复。如果你的硅没了，买不到芯片，你得重设计板子、找别的能用的。这是灾难性重设计。如果你拿不到要的RAM和想要的form factor，这就是我说的……本质灾难性重设计。你得重设计整个内脏，再保供应链、再产线建、再测、再做所有可靠性测试。不简单，所以我们才在意。（00:51:41）所以有组件层级。消费电子我们通常从硅和显示起，那是我这最长交期的。机器人里驱动器挺难买，即便只是原型。有时买个驱动器要一俩月。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is why Elon famously just starts building it all himself.
turns.zh: 所以Elon著名地直接自己全建。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Well, when you look at what he did with Tesla and verticalizing his supply chain, and famously, actually, Starlink is an even better example of this where I believe it's effectively like or and silicon chips in, product out. That's a pretty incredible factory I've heard. I'd love to see it someday. But this is where verticalization comes into play because if you have verticalized and you have a lot of the components in-house or you're building a lot of things in-house, you can actually adapt to supply chain shocks better and then famously he did. When the silicon itself was difficult to find, he was able to redesign his PCB in record time and adapt to buying new silicon. And that would be much more catastrophic for a company that had a more classic supply chain.
turns.zh: 对，看他Tesla垂直整合供应链，著名的是Starlink更是好例子——我信是'硅芯片进、产品出'。那工厂据说极厉害，我哪天想看。这就是垂直整合发挥作用的地方：如果你垂直整合、很多组件自研或自产，你能更好适应供应链冲击，而他也确实做到了。硅难找时，他能创纪录地快重设计PCB、适应买新硅。对经典供应链的公司，那会灾难得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the big decisions that I imagine you have to make when you're designing a new piece of hardware is deciding between using this available stuff, available components that are out there cheap versus, "Okay, we're going to do this something new." It's something in software too, to use the design system or do something new. How do you think about that balance when you're designing a new piece of hardware?
turns.zh: 我猜你设计新硬件时一大决策是：用现成的、便宜可用的组件，还是'好我们要搞点新的'。软件里也有，用设计系统还是搞新的。你怎么平衡？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Very simply, I use off the shelf whenever I can, especially in the prototyping phases because in the prototyping phases, which are really important phase of what we do, your goal is to show that it can work at all. Can you get a thing working? So often, it doesn't have to be the final pretty thing. It can be the ugly version. You can make an industrial design model of what the final thing's going to look like, but actually, we call it works like looks like models where you have, "This is what it's going to look like and here's how it's going to work and here's a working prototype." Humans are pretty good at this as long as, and this is a pretty big caveat, what you show could fit into the industrial design. For companies that are younger, that's not always the case, but that's what we're going for. (00:53:59): And so, in the prototyping phase, man, whatever works, off the shelf, whatever's fast, whatever you can get to quickly, and then maintain a sense of what's really going to fit in your final design. Is it capable? Are the processes and components and materials capable of actually adapting to this size, this new weight that you need it to go into? So that's part of the calculus. When you move into mass production and the final design, it depends. I mean, if I was making Matic and I could buy an off-the-shelf wheel or an off- the-shelf component, I absolutely would and fit it in. But often, what we're doing is highly custom because we have, again, one of those KPIs, "I want to be this size. I want it to be this weight. I want to be this color." And often, off-the-shelf parts aren't good enough, not because they don't work, but because they're just not exactly designed for what we're doing.
turns.zh: 很简单，能 off-the-shelf 我就用，尤其原型阶段，因为原型是我们工作的重要阶段，目标是证明'它能跑'。你能搞出东西吗？所以常常不必是最终漂亮样。可以是丑版。你可以做个工业设计模型展示最终样，但我们叫'works like looks like'模型——'这是它长啥样、怎么工作、这是能跑的原型'。人挺擅长这个，只要——挺大但书——你展示的能塞进工业设计。年轻公司不总这样，但那是我们目标。（00:53:59）所以原型阶段，啥好使用啥、现成的、快的、能快拿到的，同时心里保持'最终设计真能塞进啥'。它做得到吗？工艺、组件、材料能适应你要的尺寸、新重量吗？这是算盘一部分。进量产和最终设计时，看情况。如果我做Matic，能买到现成轮子或组件，我绝对买来塞进去。但常常我们做的是高度定制，因为又有那些KPI'我要这尺寸、这重量、这颜色'。现成件常不够好，不是因为不工作，而是没正好为我们在做的设计。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is the reason these drones are so cheap now is there's all these parts that have been innovated and built and scaled, manufactured for other things. And now, we just have all these things, and we can assemble a really cheap drone.
turns.zh: 这就是为什么现在无人机这么便宜——所有被为别的东西创新、建造、scale的零件。现在全有了，我们能装出超便宜的无人机。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对。对，正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super. You've mentioned CAD a bunch of times and it makes me think about just like CAD has been around for a long time. Just like is AI impacting the way hardware is built? Obviously, it's impacting the way software is built in a huge way. Has it changed your life and the lives of people building hardware and robots?
turns.zh: 好。你提了好几次CAD，让我想到CAD很久了。AI在影响硬件建造方式吗？显然它在大改软件建造方式。它改变你和你造硬件、机器人同胞的生活了吗？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. So I want to zoom out a little bit. So most of the hardware work goes into prototyping, into 3D CAD, so designing 3D parts and assemblies and components and making sure they work together properly, then in making sure those parts and components can be made by a vendor at quantity that is possible and the tolerances we want, and then putting those things together. So that's kind of our process. Right now, we're right at the very, very beginning of AI being able to do CAD. So I'll give you an example. Claude can do what is essentially surfaces or point clouds. This is not real CAD. Real CAD is, in my world, is dense. It has shape. It has nerves. You have an equation for how the surfaces work, and it's an entity that's designed in CAD. It's a solid entity. And so, right now, we're not quite there with AI doing CAD. (00:56:13): I think it's likely that at some point, we will be there. This will be probably one of the biggest changes for my field that we have is being able to, I hope, do rapid design and increase the speed. Now, there's a lot of really fun things to do in CAD, but like in the beginning of my career, we had to do custom screws, and we had to do the 2D drawings for everything. There's a lot of things in CAD that are not as fun. Tolerance stacks, we need them. How does seven parts fit together and are they always going to fit together properly? But it's not fun. It's not the most fun part, maybe for some of us, but not for me. And so, being able to do these things in AI would be amazing so you can focus on actually doing the fun stuff. (00:56:53): Another good thing is PCB. A printed circuit board has a lot of layers in the inside and then components that go on the top. If you've ever opened anything like a calculator or a computer and looked inside, you know what I'm talking about, these printed circuit boards. It's increasingly looking like AI can route inside of these boards pretty well, and it's looking like AI is going to be able to do some basic component selection and layout on these boards. So that's kind of where we're at right now. So we're not in a point, Lenny, where day-to-day mechanical or electrical engineering, like the meat and potatoes of it is being done by AI, but there's a huge amount that you can do as an engineer using AI in your strategy, your planning, your ability to think through the complex dependencies that you're facing. And that's what I use it for now, which is really high-level planning, asking for information. (00:57:48): When I look at who else is making a product like this, I use AI to build the databases, and they're not perfect. Certainly, a lot of times something's wrong, but it is so much faster. AI is pretty good in Excel right now, and of course, Excel is one of our favorite tools in engineering. So the ability to actually rapidly make Excel spreadsheets and change them is... It doesn't sound sexy, but actually really speeds up the design process outside of these core pieces.
turns.zh: 对。我想放大点。大多硬件工作进原型、进3D CAD——设计3D零件、组件、确保它们正确配合，然后确保那些零件组件能被供应商按我们要的数量和公差造出，再装起来。这是我们的流程。现在，我们正处AI能做CAD的最最开头。举个例子：Claude能做本质上是表面或点云。这不是真CAD。真CAD在我这世界是密的，有形状、有'神经'（nerves，应为nerve/结构），你有表面怎么工作的方程，它是CAD里设计的实体。所以现在AI做CAD还差点。（00:56:13）我觉得某天可能会到。那会是我领域最大变化之一——能快速设计、加速。我职业生涯早期得做定制螺丝、给一切画2D图。CAD里很多不好玩。公差堆叠，我们需要。七个零件怎么配合、总配合对吗？不好玩。对有些人可能不是最有趣，但对我不是。所以能用AI做这些会超棒，让你专注真好玩的。（00:56:53）另一好的是PCB。印刷电路板内层很多层，上面放组件。你拆过计算器或电脑看内部就知道。看起来AI能不错地在板内布线，看起来AI能做些基……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how Excel is always at the bottom of everyone. Anything, no matter what we're doing, we're going to Mars, there's an Excel spreadsheet that's probably driving a lot of this.
turns.zh: 我爱Excel永远在每个人最底层。无论干啥，我们要上火星，大概有个Excel表在驱动很多事。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Probably.
turns.zh: 大概。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what's interesting about what you shared is it has already impacted the work of building hardware and robots, but it's like on the verge of being transformative if it can get to real CAD.
turns.zh: 所以你说有意思的是它已经影响了造硬件和机器人的工作，但如果能到真CAD，就处在变革边缘。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. And my big question is what is it going to take? So a lot of AI is based on LLMs, which are essentially word generators, word guessers. They're more complicated than that, but that's essentially what they're doing. There's also video models that you've seen that are trained on video, but these models don't understand... They're not very good for what I need, which is I need to know, "Hey, you take a piece of paper, you fold it four times, and you do this. Where's the hole going to be when you open it back up?" These LLMs and even video models, they don't know how to do that. They don't have the ability to understand friction or weight or contact, pressure, friction, surface texture. They're just not able to do these things, and this is the core of what we need in engineering to be able to understand to build things. (00:59:26): So some world models may actually be able to do this in the future, and I suspect we may need those models to be the base of CAD and other physical engineering work. And so, my frustration, and this is like a healthy frustration, is I want Codex for engineering. I want Codex for hardware engineering, and it's extremely valuable. I've used it a lot for other things, but I want it for my field. And so, what I think it may require is new model types.
turns.zh: 对。我的大问题是需要啥？很多AI基于LLM，本质词生成器、词猜测器。更复杂但是本质在干这个。也有视频模型，但那些模型不懂……它们不擅长我要的：'嘿，你拿张纸折四次，你做这个。摊开时洞在哪？'这些LLM甚至视频模型，不知道怎么做。它们没能力理解摩擦、重量、接触、压力、摩擦、表面纹理。它们就是做不到，而这是我们要建东西的核心工程需求。（00:59:26）所以有些世界模型未来也许能做到，我猜我们可能需要那些模型做CAD和其他物理工程的基础。所以我的挫败——健康的挫败——是我想要工程的Codex。我要硬件工程的Codex，它极有价值。我用它做别的事很多，但我要它为我领域。所以我觉得可能需要新模型类型。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like an opportunity to me. I know there's a bunch of World Lab companies. Fei-Fei was on the podcast with World Labs. I think it's called World Labs. Yeah. And then, I know Google's building Gemini. So do you feel like those are the right directions or it's just like, now, we need something actually different?
turns.zh: 听起像机会。我知道有一堆World Lab公司。Fei-Fei上过播客讲World Labs。我觉得叫World Labs。对。Google在搞Gemini。你觉得那些是正确方向，还是现在就需要真正不同的东西？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I don't actually know what the latest of what Fei-Fei is working on, but obviously, she's a brilliant roboticist, and I'd love to learn more about what she's doing. So I'll have to look that up. What I've seen is that what we have right now and what models we're building are going to be part of the solution, but not all of it.
turns.zh: 我其实不知道Fei-Fei最新在干啥，但显然她是杰出机器人学家，我想多学她在做啥。所以得查。我看到的是：我们现有的、在建的模型会是解的一部分，但不全是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to robots and humanoids, something that we were chatting about this earlier, your sense is humanoid robots aren't necessarily the answer to a lot of the problems that we have and opportunities that exist. Talk about just your sense of humanoids versus non-humanoid robots.
turns.zh: 回到机器人和人形，我们早聊过，你的感觉是人形机器人不一定是很多问题和机会的答案。聊聊你对人形vs非人形的感觉。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's a hype cycle around humanoids. That doesn't mean they're not extremely interesting, and I think there's going to be winners there. But what I hear a lot is, "I want a generalist robot shape to do everything." I don't know that that works. I think that you need different types of robots to do different types of things. For example, if you've got a laptop and if you want to screw together the keyboard to the case, this is not a job I don't think, for a humanoid.
