This is a job for a dedicated robot, manufacturing robot that has been designed just to screw 10 screws into a case for this specific laptop and you want to do that 10,000 times a day or something or 10,000 times a week or something. That's a dedicated robot that's specifically intended to do that thing. (01:01:34): What I think is interesting here is you can have standard cabinet sizes for automation robots and you can have them be modifiable over time, and that's going to be a very interesting field, I think, is how do you make manufacturing robots that are adaptable and changeable, but you wouldn't want a humanoid to do that. And so, when you really go and look at a modern manufacturing facility like in China, at the top tier of tier one suppliers, there's not very many people on the line anyway. The entire printed circuit board line is essentially got no people on it anymore. The raw board is going through and getting reflowed and getting checked, and the whole thing is being done without humans unless there's something goes wrong and a human runs over and fixes something. (01:02:21): So in mechanical assembly, the same thing. These most advanced lines, they don't have people working very much. They used to have 200 people. They might have 10 now. And so, we've already kind of moved past human labor in a lot of this most advanced manufacturing. And so, we don't actually need to replace humans with humanoids. We just need more of these dedicated robots. So my suspicion is we'll have humanoids for some long-tail things that we need to do that humans are currently doing that will be important, but we'll also have robots that are for construction, robots that are for electrical work, robots that are for very low volume assembly maybe, robots for logistics, and most of them are going to look different from each other.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得人形周围有炒作周期。不意味着它们不极有趣，我觉得会有赢家。但我常听到'我要个通才机器人形状啥都干'。我不确定那行得通。我觉得需要不同类型机器人干不同类型事。比如你有笔记本，想把键盘拧到壳上，这不是人形干的活。这是专用机器人、制造机器人的活——专为这特定笔记本拧10个螺丝到壳上、一天拧一万次或一周一万次。那是专用机器人，专为干那事。（01:01:34）我觉得有趣的是：自动化机器人能有标准柜尺寸、能随时间改，那会是非常有趣的领域——怎么造可适应、可变的制造机器人，但你不会想让人形干这个。所以真去看现代制造设施，比如中国一线供应商顶级厂，线上本来就没几个人。整个PCB线基本没人了。原料板进去、回流焊、检测，全无人工，除非出错人跑过去修。（01:02:21）机械装配也一样。最先进的线，人不太干活了。以前200人，现在可能10个。所以我们在最先进制造里已经越过人力了。我们其实不需要用人形替代人。我们只需要更多这种专用机器人。所以我猜我们会有……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes all the sense in the world. What I think about as you talk about this is it feels like there's going to be this big moment when a robot can build other robots, and this CAD point you make about where once AI can develop full designs for hardware, that's going to be a big moment. Do you have a sense of just how close we are to this, I don't know, this loop that begins of robots building each other and designing each other?
turns.zh: 完全说得通。我想的是：会有个大时刻，机器人能造别的机器人，加上你那CAD点——一旦AI能出完整硬件设计，那会是大事。你对这有多近有感觉吗，这机器人造彼此、设计彼此的循环？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: If you're talking about robots building robots that are different than them usually, yes, I think that that's going to happen, but it's like the terms matter. I don't think there's going to be one robot that's going to build itself. I don't think that that's what it's going to look like. If you could say, "Hey, I want to build this thing and I want it to do this and this is kind of how I want it to look and here's a picture," the idea that you could, even as a hobbyist, go from a 2D picture to complex 3D CAD to assemblies to communication with vendors of how to make those parts and getting their feedback to iterating on that and doing a couple builds, that is possible, I think, in the future. Will it be good as good in the beginning as us doing it? No, but it will happen. (01:04:17): The biggest challenge here, Lenny, is actually the data. This CAD data is some of the most valuable IP that anybody has, and Samsung or Matic, to pick on Matic, they're not going to want to give their 3D CAD to a model vendor, to a model maker, somebody making an AI model to teach it how to make great CAD. This is proprietary. This is like the secret sauce. And so, where is this data going to come from is a big question I have, which is why I think hobbyists are a more interesting place to start where they're not concerned about the sanctity of their CAD and where it goes. They don't care. They want to make something and they want help making it faster. (01:04:55): So this is kind of where I'm interested in this starting, which is maybe a hobbyist isn't an expert in printed circuit board design. Maybe they don't care. They just want their drone to be fast and to beat this other guy's drone or whatever. This is where I think you're going to start seeing all this start, and then probably, the big incumbents are going to be slower because they have dedicated tools and a lot of IP privacy.
turns.zh: 如果你说机器人造不同于自己的机器人，通常对，我觉得会发生，但术语重要。我不觉得会有一个机器人造自己。我不觉得那是样子。如果你说'嘿，我想造这东西、想它干这干那、大概长这样、给张图'，从2D图到复杂3D CAD到组件、到和供应商沟通怎么造那些零件、拿他们反馈、迭代、做几次build——作为爱好者也能走完，我认为未来可能。一开始会像我们做得那么好？不，但会发生。（01:04:17）最大挑战，Lenny，其实是数据。这CAD数据是任何人最有价值的IP之一，三星或Matic——挑Matic——不会想把3D CAD给模型供应商、给造AI模型教它做好CAD的人。这是专有。是秘方。所以数据从哪来是我的大问题，也是为什么我觉得爱好者是更有趣的起点——他们不在乎CAD的神圣性、不在乎去哪。他们不在乎。他们想造东西、想更快被帮着造。（01:04:55）所以我觉得这会从这开始，大厂反而会慢，因为他们有专用工具和很多IP隐私。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's really interesting, this idea of what data AI models need to train on. I've been hearing that labs are buying code like GitHub repos pre 2021 because that's before AI has impacted the code because there's less and less of human-written code. And these are data labeling companies like Mercor and Surge and Handshake and things like that. It feels like this is a big opportunity that might emerge as them selling data, creating these CAD files.
turns.zh: 这'AI模型要拿啥数据训练'的想法真有趣。我听说实验室在买2021年前的GitHub repo代码，因为那在AI影响代码之前，人类写的代码越来越少。还有Mercor、Surge、Handshake这种数据标注公司。感觉这会是个大机会——他们卖数据、造这些CAD文件。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Absolutely. And one really great idea I think would be to have an AI system that can go on prem, so be inside of a data center that the company owns and then train it with their data. That, I think, could work eventually in the future, but you need a lot of this CAD data. So you're going to need a base model that has a lot of CAD data. We'll have to figure out how to do that. That's going to be very interesting. And then, we're going to have to figure out how to put it safely inside essentially the walls of companies and have them then train it on their own data. I don't know if that's going to be the equivalent of an MCP layer or what that's going to be, but this seems doable in the long term.
turns.zh: 绝对。我有个好主意：做个能on prem的AI系统，在公司自有的数据中心里、用他们数据训。我觉得未来可能行，但你需要大量CAD数据。所以你需要有海量CAD数据的基础模型。得搞清怎么弄。会很有趣。然后我们得搞清怎么安全放进公司墙内、让他们用自己的数据训。我不知道那是类似MCP层还是啥，但长期看可行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to ask you a question that my sister suggested. She's actually been a longtime VR person. She was at Oculus. She joined with the acquisition. She helped create a lot of content within VR. She's just been in the VR world for a long time, and now, she's working on other things. She wanted me to ask you, what does it take to create a robot that feels human and that humans feel connected to?
turns.zh: 我想问你一个我姐建议的问题。她其实是老VR人。Oculus收购时加入的。帮创了很多VR内容。她在VR世界很久，现在做别的。她让我问你：造一个让人觉得有人性、让人有连接感的机器人，需要什么？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: It's a great question. I'm new relatively speaking to robotics. And so, I had to learn as much as I could as fast as I could. One of the researchers that helped me the most, her name's Leila Takayama. She's an expert at this. What she explained to me is that humans have a certain expectation about how other beings are going to respond when they enter a space. When someone walks into a room, you kind of acknowledge them. You might not talk to them, but you kind of look up. There is a lot of very complex nonverbal cues that we give to each other. And if you walk into a room and a robot's just like, it's creepy, and it's easy to be creepy. I'm a little surprised with some notable exceptions how creepy a lot of these humanoids are right now. You want, I think, these devices to be non-threatening, generally speaking. You want them to appear soft, you want them to appear reactive to you. (01:07:47): You want to have a sense that they know that you're there, that they're attentive to you, that they're there to help you and make your work life easier, and you also expect them to intentionally or to show their intent before they do something. And so, one of the things I learned is if a robot just suddenly turns and does all this stuff, it scares you. But if a robot looks before it turns and then goes, it's much less alarming. So there's all these little pieces, and I recommend anyone to go look at her work. There's a lot of great research here about how to, not necessarily with a humanoid, but how to have any robot both respond properly in a social context with someone entering a room or exiting a room, but also transmit its intent physically so it doesn't surprise you.
turns.zh: 好问题。我相对新进机器人。所以我得尽量快学。帮我最多的一个研究者叫Leila Takayama，这专家。她解释给人进空间时期待别人怎么回应。人进房间，你有点认出他们。可能不说话，但抬头。有很多复杂非语言线索。如果机器人只是'……'，那瘆人，容易瘆人。我对现在一些人形有多瘆人挺意外，少数例外。你要这些设备大体不具威胁、看起来软、对你有反应。（01:07:47）你想感觉到它们知道你在、在留意你、在这帮你让工作生活更易，你也期待它们在做事前表露意图。所以我学到：如果机器人突然转、干一堆事，吓人。但如果它转前先看、再走，就不那么惊。所以这些小片，我推荐任何人去看她的工作。很多好研究：怎么——不一定人形——让任何机器人既在社交情境里恰当回应进出房间的人，又物理上传达意图不吓你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like there's a lot we can learn from Pixar and animation studios that have thought about this a long time.
turns.zh: 感觉我们能从皮克斯和动画工作室学很多，他们想这很久了。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. I actually think Pixar, Disney are probably the world's best at doing this type of design work even though they haven't done as much in physical in volume. If you look at what they do and how they show emotion, intent, approachability, engagement with their characters, they're really world-class.
turns.zh: 对。其实我觉得皮克斯、迪士尼虽没做太多物理量产，但是做这种设计世界最强。看他们怎么展示情绪、意图、亲切感、和角色的互动，真世界级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know about you, but I'm so excited to have a robot at home doing things. These videos that they're starting to put out where they're doing your... They can do dishes, at least the prototypes, they can fold laundry, they can do... It's like, yes, please come do this for me. How do you feel about robots in your house?
turns.zh: 不知道你咋样，但我超兴奋家里有个机器人干事。那些开始放出的视频——它们能洗碗、至少原型能、能叠衣服、能……就像'是的，请来帮我干'。你对家里机器人啥感觉？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So I'm into it. My partner, not so much. So I'm very lucky to have a partner who's got a high bar, which means was like never going to take Waymo, took one Waymo, and now, never wants to take anything else. So definitely willing to update her position, but it has to be pretty good. So she's in love with the Matic. It's amazing, but the bar is pretty high. So I think in order to have a home robot, it's going to have to be pretty incredible for her to be willing to have it in our home. But I take that as a challenge.
turns.zh: 我挺来劲。我伴侣不太。我很幸运有个标准高的伴侣，意思是她从不愿坐Waymo，坐了一次就再也不想坐别的。所以她愿意更新立场，但得相当好。她爱死Matic了，超棒，但标准高。所以要有家用机器人，得相当惊人她才愿放家里。我把这当挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My wife is exactly the same way. She's like, "I don't want this thing in our house with Matt. Oh, wow, this is so cute." A recent example, a self-driving Tesla. She used to be so like, "No, don't do that." It was not that great originally, and now, she's like, "I don't want to drive any other car. This just feels like absurd to drive your car. I don't want to do that anymore." It's crazy how quickly that changes.
turns.zh: 我老婆一模一样。她'我不要这东西进我们家和Matt（应为Lenny）。哦哇这好萌'。近例：自动驾驶Tesla。她以前'不，别那样'，原来说不上好，现在'我不想开别的车，自己开荒唐，不想干了'。变化多快。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So there's a big difference in my mind. This is a big categorical difference. There's a big difference between a car that is safer that drives itself versus a car that a human drives because you have an existence proof of the human driving car and you have the data. When you talk about homes, what is the delta? You have now a thing that you didn't have before doing things. So if it's bad at it, what are you relating it to? And if it's unsafe in any way, what are you relating that to? It's a much harder equation in my mind to get to a lot of people than a car where you can say, "Hey, Waymo save lives." You're going to have a fraction of the deaths using a Waymo, whether you're a passenger or you're not. When you already see people in San Francisco adapting how they respond around a Waymo versus any other car, so you're seeing behavioral changes that are based on trust, which is really cool. (01:11:18): When you're talking about a new product that hasn't existed yet and is not essentially replacing something, that's a harder sell and you have to have a different story.
turns.zh: 所以我心里有大区别。这是大类区别。自己开更安全、自动驾驶的车，和你开的车的区别是：你有'人开车'的存在证明、有数据。聊家，差值是啥？你有个从前没有的东西在干事。如果它干得差，你拿啥比？如果它任何方面不安全，你拿啥比？我觉得比'嘿Waymo救命'那种车难卖得多。用Waymo，无论你是否乘客，死亡 fraction 都低。你在旧金山看到人们围绕Waymo调整反应，基于信任的行为变化，超酷。（01:11:18）聊还没存在、不是替代啥的新产品，更难卖，你得有不同故事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that someone needs to figure out with the Tesla self-driving is often, you're at a stop and you make eye contact and then, "Go ahead. Go ahead," or someone's about to cross and you're like, "Okay, go ahead." But the Tesla just does its own thing, and so it makes you look like an asshole a bunch of times like, "Oh, I'm not driving this and in control."
turns.zh: Tesla自动驾驶常得解决的是：你停着，眼神交流然后'走吧走吧'，或有人要过'好你先'。但Tesla自己干自己的，让你几次显得像混蛋'哦我不是在开、不在控制'。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. I had that happen once. You almost want a little two arms in the front to be gesturing or you go or something. It's amazing how much we actually rely on this human connection to decide even who's going to go in an intersection.
turns.zh: 对。我遇过一次。你几乎想要前面两只小手臂打手势'你走'或啥。惊人的是我们在决定路口谁走时，多依赖这种人的连接。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. So zooming out a little bit, just what's cool about people like you is you're thinking and building things that will exist in the future. You're kind of living in the future and designing it, and you are one of the few people who has a glimpse into where things are going. So I'm curious just to ask, say in five years, what is the vision you have of what is different about our day-to-day robots, devices? Just what does it look like just roughly?
turns.zh: 对。好，放大点。像你这种人酷的是你在想、在建造未来会存在的东西。你有点活在未来、设计它，少数能瞥见去向的人。所以我好奇，比如五年后，你对日常机器人、设备不同的愿景是啥？大概啥样？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So in this job, we have this wild thing where we have to try to live in the future, and we have to try to live in the future far enough away that we can design something not only for two years from now or three years from now, but also something that will ladder up to what we want six years from now because in my field, it's a lot easier to make something and iterate on it and iterate towards a final goal than to do a one-shot thing perfectly. So not only do you have to have a sense of what the first thing needs to be like and look like, you have to have a sense of what the third thing ideally or the platonic ideal of the thing will eventually look like. So you do have to think about the future and live in the future. (01:13:06): I have this weird thing where I love to think about the future, but I'm also a skeptic, and you really want me to be a skeptic because if I think everything's going to be fine, the hardware's not going to work. You really want me to be like, "This isn't going to work and this isn't going to work and this isn't going to work," and just be worried about all these things going wrong. So this is kind of an interesting disagreement inside of me of what I want the future to look like and what I think it's going to look like and what it's actually going to look like. I'm trying to guess. And so, it seems pretty clear to me that AI is going to have a foundational change in how we work and what we do over the next couple of years, especially. You're already seeing it. Obviously, anybody who codes is not coding by hand very much anymore. (01:13:52): Any knowledge work, this is going to hit next, I think, and progressively affect our economy and our work, but it seems like the physical world is less likely to change as quickly outside of drones, self-driving cars. You're going to see more and more robots, but I'm not somebody who thinks that in five years, you're going to have 20 million robots. I don't think that it's going to be that fast. I think we have a lot of really deep work on supply chain when you do supply chain reliability, raw material access, and then we need to figure out how to make factories again in this country for high tech. So that's a lot of work, but in the interim, you're going to start seeing a lot of weird things on the street. You might see robots on the street. Have you seen any delivery robots in your world, Lenny, before?
turns.zh: 这工作里我们有个野生的事：得试着活在未来，而且得活到足够远的未来，才能设计不只两年三年后、也能阶梯式通向六年后我们想要的东西——因为我这领域，做出来迭代向最终目标，比一次做完美容易。所以你不只要感觉第一样该啥样，还得感觉第三样理想、或那东西的柏拉图理想最终长啥样。所以你真得想未来、活未来。（01:13:06）我有个怪事：我爱想未来，但我也是怀疑者，而你正想要我怀疑，因为如果我觉得一切都好，硬件就不会成。你正想要我'这不会成、这不会成、这不会成'地担心一切会错。所以这是我内心有趣的分歧：我想要的未来、我觉得会来的未来、它实际会来的未来。我在猜。显然AI未来几年会根本改变我们工作和干啥，尤其。你已经看到了。任何写代码的人不再怎么手写代码了。（01:13:52）任何知识工作，我觉得接下来会击中，渐进影响经济和工作，但物理世界似乎不那么快变，除无人机、自动驾驶。你会看到更多机器人，但我不觉得五年后你会有两千万机器人。我不觉得那么快。我觉……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like the little car things, not like anything humanoidy. Yeah.
turns.zh: 像小车那种，不是人形态。对。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So this is just going to continue happening, and I think we're just going to continue to feel like we live in the future, but safety is going to be a big key for robotics, I think. I think there's probably more change in war-
turns.zh: 对，对。所以这会继续发生，我觉得我们会继续觉得活在未来，但安全会是机器人关键，我觉得。我觉得未来两年战争的变化可能比消费电子多——

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I think there's probably more change in war than there is in consumer electronics in the next two years, for example.
turns.zh: 我觉得未来两年战争的变化比消费电子多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. What a statement.
turns.zh: 哇。这话。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I totally agree. There's nothing like war to incentivize innovation and just endless improvement and trying to get ahead of the other side.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。没啥比战争更能激励创新、无尽改进、想压过对方。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Especially when democracy is at stake. I mean, I think that we are, and I don't want to be on a high horse or something, but I do think that we're in a place where we need to think about things in the future in these terms and defend these things with our capabilities while also hoping that we never have to have hot conflict anywhere.
turns.zh: 尤其当民主攸关。我的意思是我们正处这位置，不想说教，但我确实觉得我们得用这些术语想未来、用能力守这些、同时希望永远不必热冲突。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, I have to ask you, recently you became famous, on Twitter at least, for quitting OpenAI. You tweeted that you're leaving with your brief explanation and got seven million views, 50, I don't know, 8,000 likes. What happened? Why'd you leave OpenAI? What happened?
turns.zh: 顺着，我得问你，最近你出名了，至少推特上，因为离开OpenAI。你发推说你要走、简短解释，拿了七百万阅读、五万还是八千赞。发生了啥？为什么离开OpenAI？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. So what I said in my tweet was that I have a lot of friends in the executive side of OpenAI that I care a lot about, I think are really good people. And I feel that what happened with the decision making, the speed of the decision making, the governance, and the lack of defined guardrails around the announcement of the Department of War deal is not how I thought it should have been done. And both of those things can be true. (01:16:35): And so my hope, Lenny, was that there's a third path. You see a lot of people just going along with what their company's doing and then you see some people that are kind of scorched earth about it. In this case, that didn't make sense for me. I didn't feel that way about the company. OpenAI is an amazing company and I was able to help build a robotics program there and attract some of that top talent in robotics, I think in the world. (01:17:02): And so I have a lot of, I don't know, this is a group of people I care a lot about. And you can also disagree with friends and feel like what they did isn't good and isn't right. And that's where I ended up and that's what I tweeted about. It was going to get reported on, so I tweeted before that happened.
turns.zh: 对。我在推里说的是：我在OpenAI执行侧有很多朋友，我很在乎、觉得是真好的人。而我觉得围绕'与战争部（Department of War）交易'的公告，决策方式、决策速度、治理、以及缺少明确护栏，不是我觉得该有的样子。这两件事可以都真。（01:16:35）所以我的希望，Lenny，是有第三条路。你看很多人就随公司走，又有些人焦土式对抗。这case对我没意义。我对公司不那样感觉。OpenAI是了不起的公司，我得以帮建那里的机器人项目、吸引一些世界顶级机器人人才。（01:17:02）所以我对这群人很在乎。你也可以和朋友的disagree、觉得他们做的既不好也不对。那就是我的位置，那是我推里写的。反正要被报道，所以我在那之前发了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a great opportunity to just whisper to me, what OpenAI is working on? What is this robotics device [inaudible 01:17:30], just like just between you and me?
turns.zh: 这是绝佳机会悄悄告诉我OpenAI在搞啥？这机器人设备（听不清01:17:30）就你知我知？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I wish I could say. You know, Lenny, part of the fun of our job is we get to see things before everybody else does, but part of the flip side of that is we can't talk about anything internal or any IP. What I can say is the team's really strong and I was really, really grateful for the opportunity to help. (01:17:49): But I also thought that after what happened happened, it was time for me to ... I couldn't continue to work there because you don't know what's going to happen next time. And my hope was that my decision made it easier for other folks to talk about what their boundaries were and hold them and we'll see what happens there.
turns.zh: 希望我能说。Lenny，我们工作的乐趣之一是能比大家先看到东西，但翻转面是咱不能聊任何内部或IP。我能说的是团队很强，我极感激有机会帮忙。（01:17:49）但我也觉得那事发生后，是时候我……不能再待，因为你不知道下次发生啥。我的希望是我的决定让别人更容易谈自己的边界、守住边界，走着瞧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So speaking of team building, this is something I definitely wanted to ask you about. So as I said, I asked a bunch of people what to talk to you about and someone that, I think it was maybe a colleague, former colleague, Marianna [inaudible 01:18:20]. Did you work with her?
turns.zh: 说到建团队，这我绝对想问。我说过我问了一堆人该跟你聊啥，有个人——我觉得是前同事Marianna（听不清01:18:20）——你跟她共事过？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: She's a friend. Yeah.
turns.zh: 她是朋友。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. She's a friend. So she told me that, here's what she said about you, that, "Your brilliance as a leader lies in hiring exceptional teams. I'd be curious about the kinds of people that she finds indispensable in an era where everyone is concerned about their jobs." So talk about what you've learned about just what you look for when you're hiring folks for your team.
turns.zh: 好。她是朋友。她跟我说了你对她的评价：'你作为leader的才华在于招到 exceptional 团队。我好奇在人人担心自己饭碗的时代，她觉得不可或缺的是哪类人。'聊聊你招人时看重啥、学到了啥。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. I'm lucky that I've had a lot of time, a lot of reps basically on hiring people. And so I have a strategy of hiring great people. When you're hiring for zero to one and new things or new industries, and that's what we're facing, I think with AI and robots, certainly it's very new, you can't count on having entirely people who've done the exact same thing in past lives because it doesn't exist. The exact same thing doesn't exist. Maybe you've got roboticists who've built a thousand robots, but nobody that I'm aware of has built the type of robot that can move through the world the way I'm interested in, in the millions, because it hasn't been done. (01:19:23): So you have to start thinking about how do you build a team that can do something new? And the nice thing is actually in robotics, self-driving cars, autonomous vehicles is a really good place to look because you've got the sensing stack and you've got a lot of the safety trade-offs actually. And it's a lot of the hard engineering, the hardcore engineering. So that's a place that I looked. Obviously, you want some hardcore roboticists who can do robot design from scratch. And these are really people, even though they might have a degree in something, they're really hybrid people. They're generalist people. (01:19:56): So one of the key principles I'm looking for is a lot of really strong generalists who can adapt what they've learned in other fields to a new field and people with a lot of experience building. You want some people who have experience building the thing that you're building that's new and some people who have experience scaling other things to [inaudible 01:20:14]. So you need to look at that. (01:20:15): And then with young people, this is where it gets really fun, Lenny, is the only AI native people essentially who use AI so natively that it's baked into their engineering process are 20 years old or 21 years old or 28. I mean, it's very hard to find someone who's in their 30s who can be truly fully AI native. And so we need these folks to teach us how to think. And I've had the opportunity to work with a few folks in that age range. They're approaching their problem solving completely differently because they're using AI from the ground up for everything and they're much faster actually and it's really fun to watch. (01:20:54): So figuring out how to get these AI natives to teach us, the rest of us, how they think about AI when it's, you know, we are, you and I, I think I can say are digital natives where we grew up, maybe there wasn't internet when we were really young, but we are the generation that had the first internet. We were teenagers. And we are the generation that had the first cell phones really in scale. (01:21:16): We're an important generation because we had the first, I remember freshman year at Stanford we had the first databases that you could access and you could share movies on, I think is what we did, and music on or whatever it was, but this was new. And so we were native in these things and that gave us a lot of oomph in creating new technologies for it. But we have to accept that we're not native in these new technologies and you really want some folks who are hungry and excited and want to learn who do have these skills.
turns.zh: 对。我幸运有好多时间、好多rep去招人。我有招好人的策略。当你为零到一、新东西、新行业招人——我们现在面对的，AI和机器人，确实很新——你不能指望全是有完全相同过去经历的人，因为不存在。完全相同的东西不存在。也许你有建过千台机器人的机器人学家，但我不知道有谁建过能像我感兴趣的那样在世界上移动、且百万台的机器人，因为没做过。（01:19:23）所以你得开始想怎么建能做新事的团队。好在机器人、自动驾驶、自主车是好看的地方，因为有感知栈、有很多安全权衡，有很多硬核工程。所以那是我看的地方。显然你要些能从零做机器人设计的硬核机器人学家。这些人即使有学位，也是杂交型、通才型。（01:19:56）所以我找的关键原则是有很多强通才，能把别的领域学的适配到新领域，以及很多有建造经验的人。你要些有建这新东西经验的人，也要些有把别的东西scale到（听不清01:20:14）经验的人。所以得看这个。（01:20:15）年轻人类，这最有趣，Lenny：真正AI native的人——用AI自然到 baked 进工程流程——是20、21、28岁。很难找到30多岁能……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That last bucket is a very common trend on this podcast when we talk about hiring, which is really cool as a counter narrative to there's no more jobs for young people, that junior roles are erased because of AI.
turns.zh: 那最后一类在这播客聊招人时是个很常见趋势，作为'年轻人没工作了'的反叙事，很酷。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah, I don't see it that way. I think we need them. I also think that we need to build new technologists. There's the obvious question of what happens if we don't have teams that have senior and junior people, but I think what you find when you actually build these teams is you have to have both. You must have both. The team size just might be a little bit smaller than it used to be. When this AI revolution in hardware happens, I don't know how that's going to affect the teams. That will be really interesting to watch.
turns.zh: 对，我不这么看。我觉得我们需要他们。我也觉得我们需要培养新技术人。明显问题是如果团队没有资深和初级会怎样，但建这些团队时你会发现必须两者都要。团队规模可能比从前小点。这硬件AI革命发生时，我不知道怎么影响团队。会很有趣看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I heard here is just look for a generalist that can flex based on whatever needs to be done, some mixture of specialists in scaling versus zero to one. And then the best term I've heard for this is cracked new grads that are AI native essentially, that are just doing everything AI first.
turns.zh: 所以我听到的是：找能按需flex的通才，零到一和scale专家的混合。最妙的说法是' cracked 应届生'，本质AI native，啥都AI优先。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yep. And then what we didn't talk about, of course, is mission alignment, which actually unifies a team. So if everyone coming in is aligned to the mission, that helps a lot because especially in the world of AI researchers and hardware folks, there's a lot of miscommunication because we're coming from such different worlds. And so having a sense of we're all pulling in the same direction is really important. (01:23:08): And then I rely a lot, Lenny, on my gut feel for people, assuming everything else that I'm looking for has been checked. It's hard to talk about what that means, but usually it's that spark that you're looking for in someone, that they're genuinely motivated. They're motivated by a desire to learn and by excellence, they're motivated to learn from the people around them. They're open to updating their point of view based on new information and they want to win. I mean, these are the things that really matter when you're building a team.
turns.zh: 对。然后我们没聊的，当然是使命对齐，它真正统一团队。如果进来的人都对齐使命，帮很大，尤其在AI研究员和硬件人世界，因为来自不同世界，沟通很多错位。所以有'我们朝同一方向拉'的感觉极重要。（01:23:08）然后Lenny，我很多靠gut feel看人，假设别的条件都过了。难说那意味啥，但通常就是你在人身上找的那点火苗——他们真有动力。他们被学习欲和卓越驱动，被向身边人学的欲望驱动。他们愿基于新信息更新观点，想赢。建团队时这些才真重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Just a couple more questions. Something I've been wanting to ask for a long time is you worked with some of the most legendary, successful builders, Steve Jobs, Jony Ive, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman. You don't have to go through all four, but just what's a lesson you learned from as many of these folks that come to mind?
turns.zh: 好。好。就几个问题了。我老想问的是：你跟一些最传奇、最成功的建造者共事过——Steve Jobs、Jony Ive、Mark Zuckerberg、Sam Altman。不用四个都过，但随便讲讲从这些人身上学到的教训。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: So I'll start with Sam, because most recently, Sam is really good at saying, "Why not more? Why not 100X or 10,000X? You are thinking too small. Why not think about this bigger?" And every time we talked about something important, he talked about that. And what I realized is I was thinking too small in certain areas and he was thinking globally, and having that nudge from a leader who's ambitious is really helpful, I think. So that was a big thing that I learned from him about he's willing to go for it at high volume and invest depending on ... Meaning hitting a lot of people. He's willing to think in very big numbers. That was really, really foundationally important. (01:24:54): I think for Steve Jobs it's just the bar he held for the company and for technical talent and for excellence was not wavering. It was up here, and you were either going to meet it or you weren't. And that was something that kind of washed through the whole company. When you are a young, ambitious person and you hear that something's not good enough, that can be extremely motivating actually. And it doesn't quite hit the way you would think. And if you tell somebody, "Hey, this needs to be better. You need to spend more time on this. You need to be more thoughtful about this," or, "This is not hitting our quality bar in [inaudible 01:25:35]," or something, that's impactful. And I think you never want to hear that again. So it's very, very motivating. (01:25:41): And then Mark Zuckerberg, I think that he ... I have to say he ran a company very, very well. So the way that the technical side of the company operated, the way that we had reviews, that decisions were made, the decisions were made to the lowest level possible in the company to maintain speed. I underappreciated how clean and well run ... The way that the hardware organization interacted with the rest of the company, it was very clear, "This is what we're going for. We're going to have this review. We're going to make a decision in this review. If you can make the decision without the review, you will do that. Here's the objectives for this project." (01:26:33): It was really well executed. And I think that's hard to do at a fast growing company. It's very hard to do at that level. And having him and Andrew Bosworth, the CTO, involved in the technical decisions, able to read reports that were maybe 20 pages long, [inaudible 01:26:52] the trade-offs, understand them and be able to contribute to the technical discussion, and that's just on my thing that week and they're doing that a hundred times that month, was impressive and definitely something I learned from them.
turns.zh: 从Sam起，因为最近。Sam特别擅长说'为什么不再多点？为什么100倍、10000倍？你想太小了。为啥不想更大？'每次我们聊重要事他都这么说。我意识到我在某些方面想太小，他是全球想。有野心leader的这种推，我觉得极有帮助。所以这是从他学的大事：他愿意高体量去冲、按……意为触达很多人。他愿意想极大的数字。那极极基础地重要。（01:24:54）Steve Jobs，他为公司、为技术人才、为卓越设的那条线从不摇摆。就在那，你要么够要么不够。那洗过全公司。当你年轻有野心，听到'这不够好'，其实极能激励。它不像你想的那样打击。如果你跟人说'嘿这得更好，你得花更多时间、更用心，或这没达到我们的质量线'，那有影响。我觉得你再不想听到那。所以极极激励。（01:25:41）Mark Zuckerberg，我觉得他把公司跑得极好。技术侧怎么运作、怎么review、怎么决策，决策下放到公司最低层以保持速度。我低估了那有多干净、多好运行……硬件组织和公司其他部分互动多清晰'我们要去这，我们有这场review，我们做决……'

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an incredible set of experiences and different types of places to work. I don't know if they could be more different, all these places.
turns.zh: 多不可思议的一组经历、不同地方工作。我不知道还能不能更不同，这些地方。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: I know. And I think that that's why I'm looking for this zero to one. And so when you're looking for a zero to one opportunity, it's always going to be in some place different generally.
turns.zh: 我知道。我觉得这就是为什么我找零到一。找零到一机会，通常在某个不同的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're going to be a hot commodity in this market now that you're a free agent, but on the flip side of that, I want to take us to Fail Corner. I feel like someone building hardware physical things has some great fail stories. Is there one story of something you built, something you worked on that failed and something you learned from that experience?
turns.zh: 你现在自由身，市场里会是抢手货，但 flip side，我想带你去失败角。我觉得造硬件物理东西的人有些好失败故事。有没有个你建过、干过、失败、从中学习的故事？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: This is a great question and not a comfortable one. One of my favorite failures was actually on the Quest One. It was around EVT, so halfway through the Quest One, and we found out that we had gone from five cameras to four for cost reduction. We talked a little about this. We needed to reduce the price so more people could buy them. (01:28:06): And what happened was it was right before Christmas and I heard from the lead on the team that does computer vision and he said, "Oh my gosh, the data from the cameras isn't working and we can't get a lock on where the person is using the headset." And so we looked into it and we realized that their interpretation of our spec and our interpretation of our spec was different. So in engineering, we usually use a plus or minus, like it can go up or down by, in this case I think it was 0.15mm or something like that. And in his world, he was used to having a global, it's within 0.15mm. And so we had a different interpretation of the spec. (01:28:54): Now the problem is that our interpretation of the spec meant that he couldn't meet his goals of being able to understand where the headset was in space. And so we had to do a redesign and this is at EVT. So this is pretty much when you want the engineering to be done.
turns.zh: 好问题，不舒服。我最喜欢的一个失败其实在Quest One。在EVT附近，Quest One中途，我们发现为了降本从五摄像头降到四。我们聊过点这。需要降价让更多人买。（01:28:06）然后是圣诞前，我做计算机视觉的团队负责人跟我说'哦天，摄像头数据不工作，我们锁不住头显使用者的位置'。我们查，发现他们对我们spec的解释和我们的解释不同。工程里通常用正负，比如上下0.15mm之类。他那世界习惯全局'在0.15mm内'。所以解释不同。（01:28:54）问题是我们的解释意味着他达不到'理解头显在空间哪'的目标。所以我们得重设计，这在EVT，基本是你希望工程做完时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does EVT stand for?
turns.zh: EVT是啥？

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: It stands for when we compile the hardware for the first time with everything that's supposed to be done. So final components, final materials, you're making the components on the tools, you're going to make them for mass production instead of just machining them. So it's a big deal. And so what we had to do was favor or prioritize. We had four floating cameras. We had to lock the bottom two to each other and put them on a bracket so that the relative distance from them met the spec that he needed and then let the other two float. So this was an architectural change. And this was a failure. I mean, it was a failure in understanding the spec. It was a failure in essentially the product design, but it was because of a misunderstanding of the spec. And so we were able to adapt. We actually kept the build on time and we actually shipped the product on time, but it was really stressful. (01:30:10): And it turned out that actually the new design was better because with a favored pair, you have source of truth for the space and then the other two cameras overlap onto that source of truth. And so it worked well. I thought it was a good outcome, but it was a scramble and certainly wish that we caught it four months earlier.
turns.zh: 是当我们第一次把所有该完成的硬件编译出来。最终组件、最终材料，你在工具上做组件、为量产而非只机加工。所以大件事。我们得优先级。我们有四个浮动摄像头。得把底下两个互锁、放支架上，让它们之间相对距离达标，另两个浮动。所以这是架构改变。这是失败。是理解spec的失败，是产品设计的失败，但因为误解spec。所以我们适应了。其实保住build按时、产品按时发，但极压迫。（01:30:10）结果新设计更好，因为有锁定对，你有空间真值源，另两个摄像头叠上去。所以工作好。我觉得结果不错，但是是手忙脚乱，当然希望早四个月抓到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another example of just how hard hardware is, just like you mess up a spec and like, all right, here, we wasted a week building something that didn't work and now it's like four months later still having to redo the hardware supply chain.
turns.zh: 另一例说明硬件多难：你搞错spec，'好了，我们浪费一周建了不工作的东西，现在四个月后又得重做硬件供应链'。

turns.speaker: Caitlin Kalinowski
turns.en: Yeah. It was tricky.
turns.zh: 对。棘手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the Quest One that shipped was this with the cameras moved.
turns.zh: 所以发的Quest One是摄像头移过的这版？

turns.en: Yeah. If you look, the cameras have, there's two cameras a little closer to one another in the front of the Quest than at the bottom.
turns.zh: 对。你看，摄像头，前面两个靠得近些、底部两个靠得近些。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.en: The fact that I don't remember probably means it was okay. I think we addressed it, we redesigned it. We had to change the material and the bracket. turns.zh: 我不记得大概意味着还行。我觉得我们解决了、重设计了。得换材料和支架。我觉得得用钢保我们要的公差。但成了，价格、成本、良率都行。所以我们适应了。

turns.zh: 那是史上销量最高的VR设备。对吧？

turns.zh: 好（听不清01:31:25）。好。Caitlin，我们覆盖了好广。还有啥想分享？想留听众啥？要么重申我们聊的，要么'哦这有啥想分享'。

(01:32:01): These new tools, this new way of work is scary, but if you embrace it and are daily using these AI tools right now and daily applying them to what you're doing, you'll be at the forefront of whatever comes next. turns.zh: 我觉得这可能是我们进入最激动人心的时刻之一，而且正常——我也包括——会担心害怕，但我也觉得这是人的机会，能有非凡进步、作为个体做比以前多得多的事。所以我拥抱那面。（01:32:01）这些新工具、新工作方式吓人，但如果你拥抱、现在每天都用这些AI工具、每天把它们用到你干的事上，你会站在接下来一切的前沿。所以我只想鼓励大家有创意、用这些工具、玩、搞清边界在哪，然后每次新模型出再测，因为知道我们在对付啥、边界在哪极重要。但我从没对个人力量更兴奋过。

turns.zh: 我最近多读经典。《新太阳之书》（Book of the New Sun）是本很棒的虚构书，真推荐。我想叫这名字。我有一阵没读了。我爱《达洛维夫人》（Mrs. Dalloway）。其实我觉得它是本关于转折的很有趣的书，是Virginia Woolf的战后书。所以我真爱，很棒。（01:33:12）我觉得希罗多德《历史》相当了不起。他错很多，但他也是——第一本历史书，很多case他去挖一手或二手记载。是看完全不同年代世界的方式。所以这些是我喜欢的书，第一本标题我核对后邮件你，但我想叫这名字。

turns.en: This is like very [inaudible 01:35:35] territory, but I found this list that the poet Joseph Brodsky wrote, which is a list of things you should have read in order to have an intelligent conversation in English. But what I found is it's a pretty good distillation of what we used to call the Western canon and that actually I learned a lot in my public school education and in college, but I never really learned from what you would consider the Western canon. (01:36:14): And so this is kind of in addition to that, there's some more, newer books on the list. I find it just fascinating to have something to work off of. And what I found is as I got into specifically the tragedies, the Greek tragedies, I just didn't have enough context to learn what I wanted to learn, and just reading them, I didn't have enough uptake. So I found an incredible postdoc who was willing to tutor me and I just get to ask him all these questions. He's an encyclopedia. He knows everything. (01:36:44): I could ask him what was happening in Turkey at the time of this Greek, this tragedy that we're reading and what was happening in Athens and what this tragedian might be responding to. And he can answer the question. It's really fun to have the ability to have that sounding board.
turns.zh: 这像很（听不清01:35:35）的领域，但我找到诗人Joseph Brodsky写的那张单子——为用英文聪明对话该读的东西。那是有点做作的单子。很烈。旧约、吉尔伽美什，一路下去。但我发现它挺好地提炼了我们从前的'西方正典'，而我其实在公立学校和大学学了不少，但从没真学你所谓的西方正典。（01:36:14）所以这是补充，单子上还有些更新的书。我发现就着迷有个东西可依。我深入希腊悲剧时发现：我没足够上下文学我想学的，光读 uptake 不够。所以找了个超棒的博士后愿教我，我就问他所有问题。他是百科全书。啥都知道。（01:36:44）我能问他这希腊悲剧时代土耳其在发生啥、雅典在发生啥、这悲剧家可能在回应啥。他能答。有个这种 sounding board 超好玩。

turns.zh: 我有网站，就是我名字.com。我也在LinkedIn。大家能帮我，我觉得帮着想未来。这不是单人游戏。是多人游戏。搞清我们要啥未来、想它长啥样、想那未来里人的一面是啥、想为自己留啥、想怎么增强自己。（01:38:09）所以现在我们在反乌托邦niche，一切就……感觉未来好糟。而不那样的办法是一起设计自己的未来，搞清我们想要的未来长啥样。用小说、文学、对话画出图，然后建它。我觉得那可能。
